#8399. I Caught the World-Record Striped Bass During the Eclipse of a Full Moon

Published Oct 28, 2026 10:00 AM EDT

The hottest fishing news, tips, and tactics

Somehow I knew that the full-moon night of July 16, 1981, was going to be special when I left my berth at Lake Montauk, New York, at the eastern extremity of Long Island. My only company on the 24-foot inboard-outboard was 13-year-old Eddie Turpek, who was on his first nighttime bass trip. We left at 9:30 p.m. My friend John Alberda and I had gotten word that a few big stripers had been trolled up the night before, and we felt sure that we could pick up a few fish by drifting live eels. John was fishing from his own boat, so we could cover all the likely areas and call each other on the radio if either of us hit fish.

The southwest breeze died after dark, and we were able to work our drifts perfectly at the end of the flood tide, but there was no action. However, I was marking bass on my recording depthfinder, and I was sure that they would turn on and feed sometime during the night.

It was a great night on the water. The sky was clear, and the full moon made it seem as bright as day until the eclipse started after midnight. The bass were still turned off at the beginning of the ebb. The waiting was too much for young Eddie, and he racked out in the small cabin.

Time after time I worked several spots I had fished for years. Then I tried several narrow ledges near the Great Eastern Buoy. Because bass have been getting scarcer, it has become ever more important to focus on tiny productive areas. Most of these ledges are in deeper water than we used to fish for bass. The drift usually starts over a 40-foot ledge that quickly slopes down to about a 50-foot depth. The big bass seem to hang in very specific slots where they can feed on baitfish coming over the ledge and still stay out of the full force of the moving tide.

When we first started this fishing, it was necessary to use visual ranges on buoys and objects ashore to locate a good area. Then we’d scout around the drop-off with the graph depth recorder and throw out a buoy if we marked fish on the paper. Today the miracle of Loran C has made it all a lot simpler. With the new pinpoint navigation gear, I can go back to an exact spot time after time, after which the graph recorder helps to pinpoint the proper drift for that particular stage of the tide and the wind velocity.

My tackle is simple. I use an Ambassadeur 8600 conventional reel. All the local bass experts favor reels of this type because the push-button release makes it easy to keep the terminal rig just above the bottom as the depth changes. All that’s required to put the reel back into gear is a flip of the reel handle. My rod is a custom-built job on an Ugly Stik blank. The reel had just been filled with some new 40-pound-test Ande blue mono that a friend had given me. My terminal rig consisted of a three-way swivel with a sinker (the size varies with the tide) attached on a short piece of mono, and a long leader to a 6/0 No. 92554 Mustad hollow-point hook. I’ve found that style to be ideal for this fishing. At one time I used stainless steel hooks, but I felt guilty because stainless steel hooks don’t rust out of bass that break off.

The eclipse was still going on at about 3:30 a.m. when my live eel got tapped. Usually big bass tap the eel first, and then it’s necessary to free-spool and drop back instantly so the bass can really grab the eel. I free-spooled and dropped back all right, but just as I got ready to set the hook, the bass bolted with the eel. The result was a massive backlash and a burnt thumb!

I was in big trouble, though I suspected that the fish was only a 30-pounder. The bass pulled out about 130 feet of line, right down to the knotty backlash. I couldn’t give any more line, so I walked forward from stern to bow using the bend in the rod to absorb the surges against the snarled mono. After a while I backed up and retrieved a few yards. By retrieving line this way several times I was able to get the fish within 20 feet of the boat. Then she (all trophy stripers are females) ran all the line out again, right down to the knots.

Once again I was able to stop her at the snarl and used the same procedure to get back some line. I realized now that I was dealing with a bass of respectable size, perhaps in the forties. Soon the fish was near the surface and swimming around the boat. Just as I was looking for my gaff she dived to the bottom with a great surge of power that brought me back to the backlash again. By that time I had the drag screwed down hard, but I couldn’t do anything with the fish. Perhaps, just perhaps, I thought, I’ve hooked a big fifty!

I kept turning the handle of the Ambassadeur, taking in an inch whenever it was available. I’d been fighting the fish for 10 minutes and was worried that the new rod (I’d previously used a somewhat stiffer blank) was too light. However, I worked the bass up again, and I had my four-foot aluminum-handled gaff in hand when the big cow bore down and stripped me right back to the knots again! Now I knew the fish had to be my first sixty. The only other possibility was that I had foul-hooked a medium-size bass in the body or tail. Never before had I experienced four such powerful runs against a stiff drag.

I applied maximum pressure again, and the fish rose on her own. She came up about 100 feet from the boat. I got my first real look at her finning in the moonlight. I reeled carefully, and she came in on her side. There was such a huge expanse of white showing that she didn’t even look like a bass! This was the chance I’d been working for, but when I hit her with the gaff, both rubber grips slipped off the handle and the gaff fell in the water!

The gaff’s hook was still in the fish. I grabbed the handle of the floating gaff, dropped my rod, and used both hands and my back to lift the fish into the boat. I’m six feet tall, weigh about 205 pounds, and pride myself on keeping in good condition, but it took everything I had to swing that fish aboard. As she came over the side I was knocked backward. After 15 minutes of playing her and about 600 yards of drifting, the fish was mine. She made one slap with her tail—a real boom—and she was through. I couldn’t even fit her in my 44-inch cooler. I finally realized that I had the sixty I’d yearned for!

Eddie Turpek was awake now and completely shocked by the size of the first live striper he’d ever seen. I called John Alberda on my CB radio and told him about the huge fish, but John urged me to go on fishing and catch another while they were still hitting. That’s exactly what I did, and on the next drift over the same spot Eddie’s first bass ever hit a 35-pounder. We missed a couple of others before going in at daylight for breakfast.

I was so nervous by that time that I was actually afraid to find out what the fish weighed. At Inlet Marina I showed my bass to veteran night striper charter skipper Frank Braddick, and he could only shake his head. Another night charter captain, Jack Passie, and John Alberda lifted the bass out of my boat with a boom used to unload commercial catches. At that point I had set my heart on 68 pounds, but I was afraid that I was too optimistic. The fish was weighed, and everyone on the dock shouted seventy-five pounds!

The next move was to take the fish to Montauk Marine Basin for weighing on a certified scale. Though I now have a wonderful job running a police patrol boat, I served my apprenticeship as a law-enforcement officer in the toughest areas of my county, and I was involved in many dangerous situations. But nothing shook me up more than the weighing of that bass. What if the Inlet Marina scales were off? Well, they were off, but in the right direction. The bass actually weighed 76 pounds. At 53 inches, the cow was relatively short for such great weight, but the 35½-inch girth made up for that.

Read Next: The Best Lures and Live Baits for Striped Bass

That’s the story of Bob Rocchetta’s fantastic catch in his own words as he told it to me shortly after he brought in the bass that will almost surely be the new all-tackle world-record striped bass. Though the International Game Fish Association hadn’t approved Bob Rocchetta’s record at the time this article went to press (August 1981), it is hard to imagine a refusal.

All of the tackle used in live-eel fishing complies with IGFA regulations, and there are plenty of witnesses to the legitimacy of the catch. Obviously, in this case, identification of the species is not in doubt. Most legitimate catches on sporting tackle are accepted by IGFA if the fish is fought by a single angler. If you’re interested in the rules and procedures, write to IGFA, 3000 East Las Olas Boulevard, Fort Lauderdale, FL 33316.

In 1913 an angler named C. B. Church trolled a 73-pound striped bass up from the hallowed bassing grounds in Vineyard Sound, Massachusetts, to establish an all-tackle record that has been recognized by striper fishermen ever since. To be sure, the IGFA withdrew recognition of Church’s catch in recent years during one of its periodic reviews of records. The reason was that Church’s claim had never been properly documented in accordance with current IGFA procedures. Nevertheless, that’s the record that every striper angler had been shooting at. Until July 17, they all failed.

Actually, there have been a few close calls over the years. The 73-pound record was tied during the 60s by Charlie Cinto while fishing on Capt. Frank Sabatowski’s charterboat off Cuttyhunk Island, Massachusetts. However, the IGFA didn’t recognize that fish because it was caught on wire line and hit a big plug bristling with treble hooks. Then, on October 10, 1969, Edward J. Kirker boated a 72-pounder on an eel at Cuttyhunk, a catch that received official IGFA recognition as the all-tackle and 50-pound-test class world records.

Considering that striped bass in the 60-pound class are caught every year, it’s hard to believe that the popularly accepted 73-pound record endured so long. In addition to the saltwater fisheries on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, stripers are now thriving in fresh water, and there is a real possibility that a landlocked striper may one day top all the records. As it is, the National Fresh Water Hall of Fame currently recognizes a 59-pound 12-ounce bass taken from the Colorado River in Arizona as the landlocked record.

Breaking a record set in 1913 is a remarkable feat, but that’s no reason to think that it can’t be broken again. Very big fish seem to run in cycles and are often particularly abundant as the species declines. No one caught a bluefin tuna weighing 1,000 pounds until 1970. Now quite a few well over that mark are caught every year, though the species is in big trouble. Certainly the Atlantic coastal run of striped bass is in bad shape, but trophy fish seem more abundant than ever—possibly because of lessened competition for food. There are records of stripers that weighed up to 125 pounds caught by commercial fishermen.

To striper enthusiasts, it’s a pleasure to know that the new record fish was caught by an experienced, very skilled fisherman and not by someone who relied on a charterboat captain and mate to do most of the thinking and work. Bob Rocchetta, now 32 years old, caught his first striper in the Narrows area of Conscience Bay, Long Island, when he was 13 years old. Bob had to learn the ropes from old-timers and many magazine articles and books. After graduating from college, he went to work for the Suffolk County police department, and he bought a four-wheel-drive vehicle so that he could surf cast at Montauk. He had to learn that art from scratch but did quite well with bass and bluefish by casting live eels. However, watching boats working areas well beyond his reach, Bob decided that he’d never be satisfied without a boat of his own.

Just as he was getting into a financial position to buy a decent boat, Bob got married, and instead of a boat he had to invest in a home. Nevertheless, he found an old garvey and rebuilt it and an old engine for a total investment of about $250.

To become a better fisherman Bob knew that he needed a bigger boat. He was eyeing one at a local boat dealer’s but couldn’t justify spending the family’s money on it. Then the engine in the old garvey seized up, and it looked as if he’d be beached for quite a while. Returning home dejected, Bob was met by his wife who told him that she’d just made a down payment on the boat with money she’d saved from her own salary.

The boat was soon in the water, and the fisherman was free to expand his horizons until he finally hit the giant cow bass off Great Eastern Rock during an eclipse of the moon.

This story was originally published in the November 1981 issue of Outdoor Life.

#8398. Your Ski Gear Has Been Sitting All Summer. Here’s What to Check Before You Get on the Snow.

Welcome to the most impatient time of year—for skiers, at least. The dog days of summer are behind us and we’re eagerly awaiting the first lifts to start spinning. You don’t have to sit around twiddling your thumbs, though. Instead, put them to good use getting your gear prepped for the coming season

Ski shops have transitioned from summer to winter and are firing up their tuning machines and readying their bootfitting benches—without the long wait times of the regular season. So whether you need to update or maintain your gear, follow these six tips so all that’s left to do on opening day is load your gear into the car and drive.

Nothing ruins your first ski day like searching in vain for that one glove you swore was in your boot bag. And about those boots, didn’t you leave them in the downstairs closet back in April? The first item on your agenda is to make a shred list, literally. Work down from head to toe: Helmet, goggles, buff, jacket, gloves, pants, boots, skis, poles. Knowing where you left everything is half the battle. Taking a good look at their condition is critical.

“First thing’s first, if you need to stop by your local ski shop, go now before the season starts, and definitely before the holidays,” said Otto Gibbons, hardgoods supervisor for Sturtevants Ski Shope in Bellevue, Wash. Gibbons recommends taking a good look at your skis’ bases. “If there are any noticeable points of damage, like core shots or large gouges, get those skis tuned.” Look closely to see if there are different colors of base material in the core shot because if so, water can deteriorate your ski. “Large gouges will also slow you down on the hill and even affect how your ski hooks up at a lower edge angle,” Gibbons cautioned.

Next up, check your edges and sidewalls. “If you look along your skis’ sidewall and see any area where the edge is blown out, go to your local shop because sometimes those can be repaired and save the ski from a larger fail-point of separation,” Gibbons said. If you see rust, it’s the result of not drying your edges the last time you skied. A ski tech will tune both your side and base edges to remove the rust.

“If you cannot remember the last time you took your skis into the shop, do it now,” Gibbons said. “Skis should be waxed to keep the bases hydrated and fast.” If you are someone who holds on to gear forever, know that skis typically have a life expectancy of 300-400 days of hard skiing, so if your skis no longer have snap and response, it’s likely time to get a new pair.

When inspecting your boots, first make sure they are not missing any parts like buckles. Second, check the condition of the boot soles, because if you walked around the base area from morning through après last season, your soles may be ground down and therefore your binding may not release or retain your boot properly. “If you have replaceable soles, it is important to replace them if they have worn down close to the lug of the actual shell,” said Gibbons. A ski shop tech will help you figure out what replacement soles you need.

Now for the Cinderella approach: Put your boot on and make sure it still fits. It should feel like a firm handshake. “If your foot is different than it was before due to weight change, age, pregnancy or someone dropped a piano on it, then that might mean your boot fits differently,” cautioned Gibbons. “Remember you likely haven’t had your foot in constrictive footwear for a couple of months, so don’t panic; ‘a little tighter than I remember’ is common.” And make sure your liners are clear of foreign objects: “You’d be surprised what we find, including critters,” Gibbons told SKI.

The last thing to check is the condition of your liner. Stock liners have a life span of around 60 to 120 days of hard skiing before they get that packed-out feeling. “You can put a new aftermarket liner into a shell and breathe new life into the boot if you love your skiing experience in it,” said Gibbons. “If you are outperforming the boot, or the boot is old enough to vote, start looking for a new boot.”

If you took advantage of Labor Day sales and got new skis or boots, you still need to dial them in. Go now to mount your bindings on your new skis before the wait time increases at your local shop. Also, consider the compatibility of your setup if you made any changes. “If you got new Gripwalk soles on your boots, make sure your skis, including your powder boards, have bindings that are Gripwalk compatible, otherwise the binding will not function properly with the wrong soles in it,” Gibbons said.

If you have a new pair of boots, walk around the house in them to check for hot spots. “You’ll most likely have to get them punched or worked on,” said Ian Lochhead, head alpine ski coach for the University of Colorado. Lockhead recommends that recreational skiers prioritize comfort and an appropriate flex. “Ski racers often have boots that are too tight in the toe box, but you need that part of your foot to be able to move so you can be more athletic and control your edges better. If you’re into carving, get your canting and fit issues checked out by a boot fitter before you ski in new boots.”

Skis can perform great “out of the box,” but if you get a new pair, you might need to make some slight adjustments like de-tuning the sharp tips and tails. “Skis usually come good from the factory, but we always check them,” said Lochhead. “Any shop will be able to check the base and edge bevels of your new skis, and they can even tailor them to perform best for the drier snow in the Rockies or harder snow on the East Coast.”

Outerwear takes a hit every season—from rubbing up against your dirty car when loading your skis, to tears from your favorite glades. It would be a huge bummer if you find out there’s a large hole in the back of your pants on opening day, or that your jacket doesn’t repel water like it used to.

“It’s a good idea to wash your jacket in tech wash regularly, particularly with PFAS-Free DWRs,” said Will Dobrowski, materials coordinator for Stio. “These chemistries are affected more easily by oils and stains, so when the water on the outside of your jacket stops beading up, it’s time for a wash and dry. The dryer is actually what re-invigorates your DWR to help water bead more effectively, so if you need a quick fix in the morning, throw it in the dryer for 10 minutes on low heat.”

Dobrowski recommends checking for holes on the exterior of your outerwear, followed by interior seams to make sure the seam tape isn’t peeling away, which would allow water into the jacket. You can repair small holes with adhesive gear tape, but apply it to both sides. “I throw it in the dryer for 15 minutes after patching to help the glue adhere to the fabric,” he said. Lastly, check zippers, which are common places of wear. Some brands have programs to fix issues like replacing zippers, but keep in mind turnaround times vary.

Think back to last season: Did you hit your head? “As a rule of thumb, any fall that ‘rings your bell,’ even if you don’t get a concussion, would warrant getting a new helmet,” said Jon Jay, Sweet Protection’s North American brand manager. “It’s sort of like replacing a child’s car seat involved in any sort of car crash. Do you really want to risk a more serious injury because of unseen damage?”

Barring any crashes, it’s important to check the exterior shell for any warping or cracks because the outer shell of your helmet is your first line of defense, said Jay. Also make sure that the buckle is fully functional and the straps are not worn or frayed. You can remove the inner cloth liner and wash it, but don’t remove the Mips insert if your helmet has one.

“If you’re a skier who hasn’t taken a fall in a while, we recommend replacing your helmet every four to five seasons of regular use,” Jay told SKI. “Most modern helmets are built using very technically-engineered plastics, but they will lose strength and rigidity with regular use.”

Once you know which helmet you’ll use this season, make sure your goggles are compatible, because nothing says ice cream headache like goggle gap. Inspect the foam and strap to make sure there’s a good seal against your face and then check out the lens. “If your goggle lens has scratches, cracks, or cloudiness that interferes with your vision, it’s time to replace it,” said Grady Skelton, global snow marketing manager for Smith. “If you have interchangeable lenses, a damaged lens can be a quick, easy, and budget-friendly fix.”

Once you’ve checked these boxes, there’s only one thing to do: Refresh the forecast infinite times until you finally get the news you’ve been looking for.

#8393. The Overlooked Muscle You Need to Strengthen For Better Knee Health This Ski Season

SKI Test Director Jon Jay test a pair of all-mountain skis in spring crud conditions. (Photo: Keri Bascetta)

Strong legs are essential for skiing without injury. But many traditional strength training programs focus on the bigger muscles in your lower half, including the quads, hamstrings, and gluteus maximus (your largest butt muscle).

That means the smaller guys often get neglected. And one small guy in particular–the gluteus medius, which forms part of your side butt–is worth paying attention to if you actually want to reduce your risk of knee pain and injury this winter.

Because ACL tears are among the most common ski injuries, Dr. Gregory Lichtman, an orthopedic surgeon in northern California and a physician for the U.S. women’s ski team, puts heavy emphasis on strengthening the glute medius. In his view, it’s one of the most important muscles for staying safe and skiing well.

Unfortunately, even high-level athletes can have a weak glute medius, according to Lichtman. That’s because unlike the quads, hamstrings, calves, and glute max–which can naturally get strong from activities like road running and hill climbing–the glute medius typically needs to be intentionally strengthened.

Read on to learn why this small muscle is so important, Lichtman’s favorite way to strengthen it, and other essential fitness tips for injury prevention.

The glute medius is a small muscle on your outer hip that fires up when you bring your leg out to the side, a motion known as hip abduction. It also helps control the knee by preventing it from caving inward (a position known as valgus) as you perform various movements. And it assists you in balancing on one leg, which is important when loading your downhill ski, Lichtman says.

In skiing, if you get into the back seat (meaning, you shift your body weight backwards, instead of staying centered over your skis) and the knee goes into valgus, the tibia can internally rotate, “and that’s where the ACL tears occur,” Lichtman says. Even if you don’t get a full-blown ACL tear, going into valgus when you ski can contribute to patellofemoral pain syndrome, a fancy term for pain at the front of the kneecap, Lichtman says.

By strengthening the glute medius, you can make it more resistant to valgus in the first place, which decreases your chances of both ACL tears and general knee pain.

There are also performance benefits: “A strong gluteus medius also really allows you to stand on your downhill ski a little bit more aggressively and really make a more aggressive turn,” Lichtman says. That’s because when you place most of your weight on your downhill ski (the one that’s closest to the bottom of the hill), your G-forces will want to throw you down the mountain. But having a strong glute medius–in addition to strong quads and core muscles–helps form a strong pillar on your outer hip, which ”really allows you to withstand those G forces the best,” Lichtman says.

One of the classic ways to target the glute medius is to strap on ankle weights, lie on your side, and lift and lower your top leg. Lichtman says. This exercise can absolutely strengthen your glute medius, but it’s not Lichtman’s go-to. That’s because it primarily just isolates that muscle and doesn’t mimic how we move in sports.

A better bet, Lichtman says, is to focus on exercises that simultaneously activate the gluteus medius and other muscle groups because that better resembles how we use this muscle during athletics. His favorite exercise that ticks that box? The monster walk. Not only does this move really fire up the gluteus medius, but it also works the core, hamstrings, quads, and glute max, he says.

Incorporate this exercise into your workouts three days a week, with at least one day off in between each session so that you give the muscle the downtime it needs to recover and build back stronger. To stave off boredom–and also work different parts of your hips and quads–incorporate different variations of the monster walk throughout the week. For example, instead of stepping straight out to the side, step forwards and backwards, or diagonally forward and diagonally backwards. As long as you have good form and keep your legs spread apart so that you feel tension from the band the whole time, “all directions can be effective,” Lichtman says.

Lichtman suggests doing monster walks during both pre-season and throughout ski season. “One of the big pitfalls is that we will all get ready for ski season, and then taper off our dry land training,” he explains. “If you’re one of the fortunate few who can ski five or six days a week, you’re probably getting enough exercise, and you probably don’t want to stress your body out any more than that. But for those of us who are skiing two to three days a week, finding some time to do some cross-training and continue to work on our core and our hip abductor strength is really important because those are the less commonly used muscles during skiing.”

Once this exercise becomes easy, level up the challenge by using a stronger resistance band.

A strong glute medius can keep you safe on the slopes. But it’s not the only fitness-related aspect of injury prevention.

Having a strong core and quads, along with good overall endurance, is also key. That’s because one of the essential components of an ACL tear pattern in skiing is getting kicked into the back seat. And while the gluteus medius helps guard against knee valgus in this position, it doesn’t prevent you from getting into the back seat in the first place, Lichtman explains. What does help? Having strong core and quad muscles, plus overall endurance. This trifecta, Lichtman says, is “fundamental” to staying out of the back seat.

On the endurance front, the goal is to be as fresh after lunch as you are after breakfast, Lichtman says. “Fatigue is definitely a risk factor for ACL tears,” he says, explaining that fatigued skiers more frequently get into the back seat and sustain injuries than those who aren’t zapped. So make sure your dryland training doesn’t just focus on lifting weights: “A balance of endurance and strength training is integral for a skier preparing for ski season,” Lichtman says.

How a former gang member found a different kind of vigilance in the Montana wild.

One summer evening, I was hiking a trail near Marias Pass in Glacier National Park, returning to the car after a few hours of wildlife photography at a lake— nothing but deer and mosquitoes to show for it—when I noticed something blondish-brown moving toward me. It barely registered. I felt relaxed, though, truthfully, I’m never fully relaxed.

A grizzly cub, big as an overgrown Saint Bernard. I was fascinated—until reality hit. The mother wouldn’t be far behind.

I turned toward the trail ahead. And—boom—there she was. Running at me, big and fast and flat to the ground.

#8389. How to Sharpen Broadheads: The Techniques and Gear You Need to Know

Published Oct 28, 2026 10:39 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

During my bowhunter safety course, the instructors showed us a video of Fred Bear sharpening a broadhead with a mill file while discussing the importance of sharp broadheads. The instructors then showed the class the difference between sharp and dull broadheads using rubberbands to represent blood vessels. The sharp heads popped the bands without effort and the dull heads pushed them to the side. Since I was already a knife nerd and obsessed with keeping my knives sharp, the lesson about sharp broadheads stuck with me. I believe it is the most important component besides shot placement for making an ethical kill.

If you want to ensure your broadheads are absolutely deadly, here’s how to sharpen just about any head, whether it be an old-school Zwickey or Bear, a single bevel, three or four-blade, replaceable blade, or mechanical broadhead.

Use a permanent marker to color the bevel. Then adjust the angle of your sharpening system until you’re removing the marker evenly from the bevel. Matching the angle makes sharpening faster and removes less material than setting a new angle.

Once you have the angle, use light pressure to remove material until you raise a burr. A burr is a thin piece of metal right at the apex of the bevel (see graphic above).

Then flip the broadhead and raise a burr on the other side. Move to a finer grit and repeat the process until you no longer feel a burr.

You can stop sharpening once the burr is removed, or you can polish the edge by stropping. The key to stropping is to match the angle and use light pressure.

When a broadhead is fresh out of the package or still relatively sharp, you don’t need to sharpen it. Instead, hone it. Honing doesn’t remove steel — it polishes and realigns the existing edge.

You can use a ceramic rod, a strop, the bottom of a coffee cup or the edge of your car’s window to hone an edge. As with sharpening, match the angle and use light pressure. Alternate sides when honing.

A sharpening stone is excellent for all types of heads. You’ll need a two-sided stone or a dual-grit diamond stone. The stone should have a coarse side for removing edge damage and and a fine grit for honing. I use a Fallkniven DC4, which is a quality, pocket-size stone. A leather strop is optional, but it will really take the sharpness to another level. I highly recommend a large, wood-backed leather strop, which works wonders for knives and broadheads.

A belt sharpener with various grit belts is the fastest way to sharpen fixed and replaceable blade broadheads. I use a Work Sharp Ken Onion with the Blade Grinder Attachment, but a regular bench belt sander would work with belts up to 800 grit.

On a belt sharpener, you will create a slight convex edge, which is generally tougher and more resistant to rolling and chipping. With some practice, you will be able to get mirror-polished edges that easily shave hair.

I like to use an old arrow that’s cut to about 8 inches to hold heads while sharpening. This “handle” gives extra control and is especially useful when using a belt sander.

You won’t see me wearing gloves in the photos accompanying this article, but I’m a professional knife sharpener with a lot of experience. If you’re new to sharpening, I recommend wearing thin leather gloves or cut-resistant gloves while sharpening broadheads. That’s because it’s usually necessary to hold broadheads by one of the blades, which obviously adds a risk of nicking yourself.

The classic two-blade broadhead is fairly easy to sharpen. It’s essentially the same process as how to sharpen a knife. You can use a stone, belt sander, or fixed-angle system for these heads.

The most challenging part will be keeping a steady angle while making your passes on the stone or belt. I recommend everyone learns to freehand sharpen on a stone because it’s a great skill to have, and it’s very fast once you get the technique down. A stone is also much easier to pack on a hunting trip than a sharpening system. But, if you want guaranteed results, a fixed sharpening system like the Work Sharp Precision Adjust is the easiest way to get super sharp heads.

With a fixed-angle sharpener or freehand, you’ll want to match the factory sharpening angle. It’s helpful to color the edge with a permanent marker so you can see where you are removing material. Adjust the angle until you’re removing material evenly across the bevel.

With any of the sharpening tools, use slow, even passes until you raise a nice burr on the whole edge, then repeat on the other side. After you’ve raised a burr on all four edges on both coarse and fine stones or belts, you can move to a strop.

Stropping polishes an edge, and it’s a great thing to do between hunts to keep broadheads sharp. Most strops have two sides so you can apply a coarser compound to one and a finer to the other. Stropping is a lot like sharpening on a stone, except you’ll use much lighter pressure. Hold a consistent angle and drag the broadhead across the surface. Be sure to pull the blade with the edge facing away from you, so that you don’t cut the leather.

Sharpening single bevels is a bit different than other heads, but it’s actually pretty easy to get the hang of it. Lay the bevels on your stone and start making passes — the whole bevel should be in contact with the stone. You will easily feel (and see) when you have the correct angle.

Flip the broadhead to the flat side and use a strop to remove the burr you created — don’t use a stone. A few passes on the strop will buff away the burr, and you will be left with a very sharp broadhead.

As with two-bladed fixed heads, it can be helpful to color the whole bevel in permanent marker to see where you are contacting the head with the stone. It will also help you see low spots so you can flatten the factory grind if needed.

I don’t use belt sharpeners on single bevels, because they aren’t designed to be convex grinds. They work best at a flat angle, so stones are really the only way to go for these types of heads. They can also be clamped into guided systems and sharpened that way, but stones are still the most effective in my opinion.

A three-blade broadhead may just be the easiest broadhead to sharpen, and a stone is all you need. Simply lay the broadhead down so that two of the blades are on the stone, and one is sticking up. Keep the blades in contact with the stone and apply even pressure as you run the head back and forth on the stone. Check to make sure you have raised a burr on the whole length of both edges, and once you have, just rotate the head, and do the next side the same way. One more rotation, and you will have raised a burr on all six edges. Now repeat this on the fine stone and then strop.

When you’re stropping, be sure to have the tip trailing, otherwise, you’ll end up with a big V shaped slice in the leather. There are no tricks with these heads. They’re easy to hold, easy to sharpen, and it doesn’t take much practice at all.

I don’t recommend doing these on a belt unless the belt is wider than the widest spread on the broadhead. It’s do-able, but you can also easily ruin a head on a belt sander.

When a mechanical becomes dull you can replace the whole broadhead or its blades — both can get costly and leave you with a false sense of security. In Outdoor Life’s broadhead test, many of the mechanicals were sharp, but had dull spots, especially toward the ends. So it’s wise to improve on their out-of-the-box sharpness with a fine stone or strop.

The difficult part of sharpening a mechanical is holding the blades still. But, with a little practice, you should be able to hold the head still while you run the stone back and forth across them. A sharpening stone with a base makes the process easier because you can use both hands.

Move the stone back and forth until you have raised a burr along the length of the edge, then flip it over and do the other side of the edge. After you have raised a burr on both sides of both blades, repeat the process with the fine grit stone/side, and then finish with a strop. Remember to always have the edge trailing when you run it on the strop, otherwise you will cut the leather.

I don’t recommend using a belt system for mechanical heads because it’s just too easy for the blade to fold and possibly injure you, or mess up the broadhead. Also, many mechanicals have replaceable blades, so if you’re struggling, try taking them out for sharpening.

Some people laugh when they hear about sharpening replaceable blades because, well, you’re just supposed to replace them. Right? Again, these aren’t always that sharp out of the box, and why replace them if they can be reused? Stretch your hunting dollar a bit further and sharpen them.

For replaceable blades, I always remove them from the head, and sometimes if they are really small, I will hold them with needle nose pliers. The process for stones or belts will be the same. Hold the blade at a steady angle and raise a burr either by moving back and forth across the stone, or across the belt.

Repeat for the other side, and for each blade. Work through this process with finer abrasives, and then strop to a nice polished edge. Try to match the angle that is already ground into the blade as closely as possible. If the blades have been used, examine the blades carefully to make sure they aren’t bent. A bent blade will need to be replaced. If the blades are new, you may only need a few passes on the fine stone, or a minute on the strop to really get them sharp.

Replaceable blades are generally made from softer steel because it’s less expensive, takes a good edge, and doesn’t need to hold an edge long. So, sharpening (removing and reshaping material) usually happens pretty fast.

Replaceable blade heads usually have a sharp ferrule up front to initiate the cut and break bone ahead of the blades. Many of the ferrules can be dressed and touched up on the stone as they get nicks and rolls in the edges. The sharper the leading edge of the head is, the more likely you are to get a pass through. Stones are generally better for this because the flats on the ferrule can be laid flat on the stone and run back and forth until the edges are sharp again. A belt will have the tendency to flex and convex the tip and trailing edge.

Yes. Sharp heads lead to more bleeding, better penetration, and a much higher probability of having two holes pumping blood, rather than one.

First off, slow down. Most beginners rush the process. Slower passes are easier to control. Also, you can use your fingers as depth guides. Hold the broadhead in way that your fingertips are just touching the stone when the head is at the correct angle. Keeping your fingertips in contact with the stone at all times will help you know that your angle is consistent.

The most obvious will be bends or cracks in the blades or ferrules. Less obvious is when blades thin out. Many mechanical blades are thin and relatively weak to begin with, so sharpening them several times, especially if you have to grind away edge damage, can thin the blades out to a point where they are too weak.

Broadheads are like bullets in that they are what actually does the killing during a hunt. There is a whole lot that goes into delivering a bullet or broadhead to the intended target, but the moment of truth happens when the payload is delivered. Having the sharpest broadhead possible will help you get more game, give you more confidence, and give you shorter blood trails. Whatever head you choose for your hunt, just make sure its razor sharp.

Drew Conover is a contributor at Outdoor Life. He writes mostly gear reviews and how-to articles on survival and navigation. He lives in Upstate New York with his wife, two daughters, and a goofy dog.

Scott Einsmann is Outdoor Life’s gear editor. He oversees the gear team’s editors and writers who are subject matter experts in bows, knives, hunting, fishing, backpacking, and more. He lives in Richmond, Virginia with his wife and two bird dogs.

#8386. Freddy Krueger Deer: These Are the Monster Bucks That Still Haunt Our Nightmares

Published Oct 28, 2026 1:01 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

When I first started working for Outdoor Life as a young, junior editor, I had a recurring nightmare that went like this: I’m sitting in a ground blind with my new boss (the editor-in-chief). A buck materializes out of the woods. He has an impressive rack, but a small body—an absurdly small body. He’s the size of Boston terrier. The editor-in-chief sees nothing strange about this and whispers to me, “Shoot him.” So, I draw my bow and shoot…and miss the tiny Booner buck. But following close behind this dwarf buck is another mini buck, so I nock another arrow—and miss that one too. These miniature bucks keep coming and I keep shooting—and keep missing. Somehow my quiver has endless arrows and the editor-in-chief sitting next to me has a limitless capacity for disappointment.

The thing is, this nightmare is based on a true story. Or at least a combination of a few true stories. Hunt whitetails long enough and you’ll miss a big one. Some of these misses can be explained by logic: a tree branch deflected the arrow; it was a tough shot on a moving deer; the damn buck jumped the string.

Other misses have no logical explanation whatsoever. They happen because adrenaline and panic overcome rationale thinking and highjack our motor skills. These misses happen because of buck fever. If you miss a big buck in this fashion, it will haunt you forever. These are four buck stories that still haunt our dreams—no, nightmares—to this very day.  —Alex Robinson

Nowadays, when you live three hours from your hunting camp, trail cameras help keep tabs on deer movement. Prior to that, you had hunting buddies who kept an eye on things for you. For me, that was Tommy Cormier. You’ve never heard of him, but he was the best deer hunter I’ve ever known. He basically lived in the woods from October until January. When he saw noteworthy bucks, he’d call to give me the scoop.

“So, here’s how this needs to go,” he told me one day. “Next week is opening day. I’m going to tell you where to sit, how long to sit, where to look, and what you’re looking for. Well, he’s a perfect 10-point with double drop tines. That makes him a 12. He’s wide, has incredible mass, and is just a stud that really likes apples. I’ve never seen a better deer.”

I, of course, didn’t believe him. Dutifully, though, on opening day I parked myself at the base of the snowy tree that Cormier described. By 5:30 a.m., I was comfortably in place. Shotgun barks seemed to come from all directions until they subsided around noon time. Chilled, but mostly bored, I decided to take a walk. I slung my Mossberg 835 12-gauge over my shoulder and slowly began a stillhunt.

I took 10 steps (I know because I counted and recall each one) before catching a flash of movement to my left. It was a nanny (mature) doe running right toward me. I had an antlerless deer permit, raised my shotgun, and snicked off the safety. Behind her, though, was another flash of movement. Just before pulling the trigger on the doe, I saw antlers—a giant set of antlers. It was the double-drop 12-pointer and he was awe-inspiring. A giant if there ever was one.

My first shot was an open 60-yarder. Clean miss. No excuse. The two deer paid no attention whatever and continued to run at me rather than running away. By the time the buck had closed to 40 yards, I’d fired all my slugs and gingerly reloaded. With my final round, I fired at the buck as he was standing-still buck at 25! He ran off with no indication whatsoever that he’d been hit. I watched, listened, and then puked for 15 minutes.

With as many hunters that were in the woods, I was relatively certain that someone else would have run into that giant buck.

With a light skiff of snow on the ground, I felt certain that at some point during my follow-up I’d find a speck of blood. Nothing.

So where did the double-drop 12-pointer get off to? I never saw nor heard of him again. No dead-head, no sheds, no other sightings of him exist, except for in an occasional nightmare. —Gerry Bethge

I don’t remember shaking at the shot, though I must have. I do know the buck came in on the same trail the deer always do. I heard him first, then saw him. He dipped behind a big oak trunk, and when I saw him again, I knew exactly who he was. We had just one trail camera photo of this deer, a distant shot on a gloomy day of an absolute giant.

Don’t look at his antlers, I thought, even as I looked at his antlers. They were hard to miss: curved and white and sweeping out to his nose and high above his head. This would be the biggest buck ever killed on our family property.

His shoulders were broad, his body dark. And he was moving fast. When he finally paused for just a moment, near enough to shoot with a bow and quartering to me, the crosshairs in my riflescope settled on the point of his shoulder. Someone shouted “NOW!” inside my head, the gun went off in my hands. The buck spun on his heels. The plot was so small and he ran so fast that by the time I jacked another round into the chamber, I got one last parting view of his antlers disappearing into timber.

That night and the next morning, I didn’t find a single speck of blood. Nothing to suggest a deer hunter had been sitting here when a shooter buck walked in front of her. Just the churned-up leaves and wet earth where the buck ran out of my reality and into my nightmares. The trail camera he’d cruised by just before I missed didn’t just whiff on one photo; the entire card was blank.

Since then, our trail cams have been plagued with problems: condensation, missed triggers, neon pink static. Perhaps they’re cursed. The deer they do manage to capture look insubstantial as they lurk on the edges of the frames, white specters against the black fields. A critter that resembles a cow with antlers has been haunting my favorite spots. It’s always in the dead of night, and each photo is too dim, too smudged, too foggy to tell much about the buck. In one, the big body is clear enough, but his antlers disappear into the gloom. Another will show, startlingly close in the corner of the photo, the curve of a familiar main beam.

But none of this is proof that the buck has returned. The only way to know for certain is to walk into the dark woods and wait to see if he’ll show himself. —Natalie Krebs

The shot looked perfect. Ok, maybe just little high. I was sitting in a ground blind alongside videographer Matt Arkins reviewing footage of my crossbow bolt disappearing into a Kansas buck—the biggest buck I’d ever shot.

The deer (an easy 165) had come in just before the close of legal shooting light. Matt had spotted him first and had gotten very, very excited. “Big buck, big buck. I’m serious,” Arkins whisper-yelled at me. “He’s coming in. He’s the one. Get ready. High double lung.”

I steadied my crossbow and found the buck in my scope. I tried to flick on the reticle illumination, but realized the batteries were dead. No matter, I could still see my 40-yard holdover just clearly enough against the buck’s profile. He came to what I thought was about 45 yards. Through the falling darkness, his body started to blend in with the tall grass behind him. No matter, I could still see his backline. Just drop the 40-yard holdover a tad below his backline and squeeze, and…SCHWHICK. The crossbow fired. The buck kicked and disappeared into the grass.

Matt and I celebrated. We called one of our hunting buddies to share the news—we’d done it. Unfortunately, premature celebration and relief is part of any true nightmare. As we played back the shot on Matt’s camera we noticed my arrow had hit a little high. We waited a bit and then went to look for blood. We paced off the shot distance and discovered he was just inside 40 yards, not just outside 40 yards. We found decent blood to start, but then the trail evaporated. The dread began to sink in.

The next day we grid searched. We called in a blood tracking dog. We even got a ride in a plane to fly over the area. It turns out that I, in fact, had not killed the biggest buck of my life. I’d wounded him.

Three days later I got a text from Matt with a trail camera picture of the buck, alive and well, heading to a feeder—though he had a scar on his back over an area that bowhunters like to call no man’s land. “He’s still out there,” Arkins said. All I could think to reply was: “Yes. Yes he is.” —A.R.

I was home from college on Thanksgiving break with the goal of filling my Connecticut shotgun tag. I grabbed the Remington 870 youth model that I had outgrown five years prior, a couple slugs, and my blaze orange. I had access to a piece of private land where I set up on the edge of a field that was about 200 yards wide—way too far for me to shoot with my open-sighted slug gun. But at the time, I was an inexperienced hunter who thought sitting field edges was the way to go. In that magic last hour of daylight, I caught movement across the field. With my naked eye, I could tell it was a buck—a big one.

Before I continue with the story, you need to know a little background. I had spent many frustrating seasons trying to kill a deer on my own and had yet to be successful. Killing this buck would be a turning point for me. I could feel the magnitude of the moment.

The question was, how would I get close enough for a shot? Well, after the buck was done working the scrape, he moved left behind a rise in the field. The rise was maybe 15 feet in elevation, but enough to completely hide him. I jumped up and sprinted—while keeping my head low—to the base of that rise and began creeping toward the crest. As I popped over the top, the buck was standing broadside 50 yards away. We looked at each other. For an instant I imagine we both felt the same bit of surprise. I leveled the shotgun and shot.

Notice I didn’t say, I leveled the shotgun, aimed, and shot. The deer bounded off, looked back at me from the edge of the woods, and kept going. No blood to be found, not a strand of hair. The only thing left in the field was a distraught college kid, pacing back and forth, muttering to himself, and suffering over what might have been. My chest tightens every time I think about that hunt. I’ve shot plenty of deer since then, and some nice bucks too, but none of them bound through my memory as often as the first big buck that I missed. —Scott Einsmann

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.

#8381. The Best Rifle Scopes for Deer Hunting, Tested & Reviewed

Published Oct 28, 2026 4:04 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

I grew up deer hunting in the woods of north-central Wisconsin where a 100-yard shot would be a long one. We needed only a simple 3-9X riflescope that gathered enough light to let us shoot a half-hour after sunset. In other words, any streamlined riflescope with decent glass would work just fine.

A lot of deer hunters still hunt this same way. But riflescope offerings have grown exponentially. So the best riflescope for deer hunting really depends on where, and how, you intend to hunt.

With this roster of scopes I’ve attempted to select a good variety of styles that will work in the northwoods, the open country of the West, and everywhere in between. All of my picks are based on data from in-depth testing conducted by OL’s Optics Editor Andrew McKean and our Gear Editor Scott Einsmann. I focus mostly on affordable options, but there are a couple high-end picks included, too.

The Burris Fullfield is a classic deer scope, built on a 1-inch tube with capped turrets and a second-plane duplex reticle. It’s a simple, capable scope that’s offered for under $300.

​This scope has some nice features, including distinctive red accents on the power-changing ring and turret dials and re-zeroable turrets. But it’s not perfect either. It has a distracting greenish coating that’s especially noticeable in low-light conditions. Its turret indexing is so tiny that it’s hard to confirm when you’re zeroed.

But for a good image, plus simple and repeatable controls, the Burris Fullfield 3-12×42 checks every box for the workaday deer hunter.

Nightforce is known for building battle-ready riflescopes for long-range precision shooting. But their new NX6 product line is designed specifically for hunters. I used the 3-18X50 F1 version with a MIL reticle on an elk hunt this fall and found it to be an excellent open-country hunting scope. It had strong image quality and low-light performance. It’s a hefty scope, but not absurdly so, like some other precision optics.

One of the key features of the NX6 line is the new FieldSet turret system. Once you’ve established your zero, any simple tool — a coin, knife, or flat rock — will loosen the exposed turret cap, allowing you to reset your zero and set the zero stop. The stop can be set a full revolution above zero, or 2 MILs.

One of the many cool things about this system is that any NX6 model except the 1-6x can be converted from capped to exposed turret, and the standard exposed turret can be traded for a custom BDC turret. It’s another indication that the NX6 is positioned to be the ultimate versatile scope family.

The scope comes with a versatile illumination system that lights up the entire reticle. This is a relatively advanced and expensive scope, but for spun-up riflemen who are looking to shoot deer at longer ranges, it’s an excellent option.

The latest incarnation of Trijicon’s legendary AccuPoint line, this durable LPVO is designed to withstand the recoil of big-bucking magnums. Its always-on illumination doesn’t require a battery to fire. Its balance, style, and grit befit a bespoke rifle that’s imagined as an heirloom but used as your ride-or-die hunting gun.

Instead of relying on a battery, the Trijicon’s illumination is activated by sunlight that hits the windows of a fiber-optic receptor and translates photons into intensity of a fine 0.25 MOA green dot at the intersection of a bold second focal-plane duplex reticle. In low-light situations, the element tritium does the work of the sun and supplies the energy to light up that aiming point.

It’s an elegant and durable system that’s optimized for this 1-8×24 build, which neatly fits every AR and straight-wall cartridge carbine made. The scope’s Dangerous Game BDC reticle in MOA is built for close-in and medium-range target work. The tough detail is its price, which is steep.

The excellent glass, tight but understated controls and tasteful lines elevate the Trijicon to a level of sophistication that most grubby LPVOs can’t reach.

The TANGO-MSR Compact brings plenty of versatility in a package that measures 8.4 inches and comes pre-mounted on a very good cantilever unimount for the screaming price of $399.

The glass in this scope isn’t great, but everything else about this little marvel is spot-on. The second-plane arrangement in the TANGO-MSR is simple and useful. The inverted-horseshoe center aiming arrangement blazes bright in daylight conditions, and the BDC grid is useful for placing bullets with precision on targets out to 500 yards. The only real tradeoff is that the scope must be set at its highest magnification for the bullet-drop subtensions to be accurate.

We put the scope through a battery of close-range fast-fire drills, and atop an AR carbine, then we slowed things down and rang steel out to a quarter-mile with the scope. It performed admirably in all cases.

The TANGO-MSR is optimized for AR, but it would be great on a straight-wall cartridge carbine or muzzleloader.

The Crossfire HD line, slowly replacing the Crossfire 2 line, has a scope for every hunter, from a handy LPVO to a big 6-18×50 model to this mid-mag optic that’s optimized for America’s deer hunters.

The 4-12×44 model is priced at only $300, and is an excellent budget option. It’s built on the second focal-plane arrangement and with MOA-based aiming points. There’s the classic Dead-Hold BDC that’s a non-illuminated plex design with three bullet-drop references and windage hashed. Or you can opt for an illuminated version of that reticle, with a pin-point illuminated center dot for a $50 upcharge. Or you can go old-school and use the Widerange Plex, which is basically a German #4 duplex without illumination.

The glass in the Crossfire HD line didn’t blow us away, but the magnification range is right in the sweet spot for whitetail hunters, and we found it to be an easy, simple, and budget workhorse.

“I think your average hunter would take this over the other $300 scopes in our test. It’s worth that price all day long,” noted Outdoor Life optics tester Todd Netto.

For $450, you get some great features and performance from the V3. It is offered in three versions of its second-plane reticle build, a non-illuminated No. 6 plex and both non-illuminated and center-dot illuminated versions of the SHR (it stands for Smart Hunting Reticle) hash-style design with MOA-based holdover and windage references. The illuminated version has a crisp center dot that shines with a red illumination.

These new Zeiss scopes are no longer made in Europe. They’re sourced in Asia, but if that suggests a decline in optical performance or brand integrity, worry not. These are excellent scopes that use premium components. Also, they’re designed for the American hunter.

For a price-point scope, Bushnell’s R5 has some surprisingly sophisticated features. The most useful is its second focal-plane DOA-LRH800 reticle.

The modified tree-style reticle is extremely tunable, meaning that for shooters and hunters willing to invest the time, the Bushnell Ballistics app can produce customized drop tables for your specific load and magnification setting. Not too shabby for a $250 scope.

The R5 doesn’t have quite the smooth and confident controls of its big sibling, the R7 introduced earlier this year, but it’s a more responsive and precise build than most scopes in its price range. If you’re willing to spend a little more, consider the R7 line which won our 2026 Editor’s Choice award for best all-around hunting scope.

This is a throwback deer scope in all the best ways. It’s hardy and durable. It’s simple and reliable.

The Maven brings a second focal-plane MOA-based reticle that’s clean and easy to see. The heart of the scope is the wire-frame CSHR-W reticle, which provides 20 MOA of windage references on the horizontal stadia at 10x, along with 20 MOA of elevation holdover. At $425, the Maven is priced in a sweet spot for deer hunters.

Sometimes you just need a simple, old-school optic for your deer gun. This stripped-down fixed-power scope from Athlon is designed for muzzleloaders, but it could just as easily work on a lever gun.

There’s remarkably little to say about this Talos HMR. Its 1x magnification is pretty solid, without the fishbowl distortion of some low-power scopes. The duplex reticle is proven. There are no illumination or parallax controls to worry about.

All that simplicity holds the Athlon back, of course. It’s not going to help you reach out beyond 300 yards to ring a steel target, and it’s not going to offer any windage or hold-over marks. But it should be durable and fast to target at shots at deer inside 100 yards.

Leupold is filling out its product line with this 4-times zoom ratio family that bridges the gap between the VX-3HD and the VX-5HD. Significantly, the VX-4HD scopes feature Leupold’s excellent push-button 2-revolution CDS-ZL2 elevation dials, and not the toolless Gen2 turrets that it’s rolling out with its other premium scope lines.

You’ll recognize many of the features of the VX-4HD line. It’s built on a second focal-plane system with a fairly standard selection of reticles: duplex, Wind-Plex with 1 MOA hashes extending to 10 MOA on either side of the center crosshair, and illuminated FireDot Twilight Hunter.

​But the new family has upgraded optics, delivering a bright, crisp, and vibrant image. An important point for deer hunters: the 4-20×50 won our low-light test, thanks to the big 50mm objective lens and the excellent glass and coatings. Its removeable elevation turret can be traded out for a free custom ballistic dial tuned to your own bullet and load (second CDS dials cost $80). The scope itself costs about $1,000, with illumination adding another $100 to $200, depending on configuration.

Sure there might be brighter, more powerful, and more feature-rich scopes on the market. But those optics aren’t what most deer hunters want, or need. The best deer scope is functional, reliable, and simple. Hopefully, it’s affordable too. So that’s how we built this list of scopes. For more detailed coverage on how we conduct our riflescope testing, check out our reviews on the best LPVOs, Best Hunting Scopes, and Best Precision Rifle Scopes.

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.

Andrew McKean is Outdoor Life’s hunting and conservation editor, drilling into issues that affect wildlife, wildlands, and the people who care about them. He’s also OL’s optics editor, helping readers to make informed buying decisions.

#8380. “I Was in Disbelief.” Crossbow Hunter Takes Massive 250-Class, 290-Pound Nontypical Buck

Published Oct 28, 2026 4:40 PM EDT

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

Mike Ferriman, a 42-year-old agricultural sales rep from Caledonia, Ohio first learned of a giant buck this year on a farm he has permission to hunt on September 22. A few trail camera photos revealed that the massive whitetail’s rack was similar to a heavy buck he had photos of last year on the same farm.

“But this year his rack had just blown up,” Ferriman tells Outdoor Life. “There were some familiar kicker points to the rack, but it was a lot bigger and heavier.”

Ferriman didn’t have many trail cam pictures of the deer before he got into a 21-foot-high ladder stand on the farm in heavy timber the afternoon of October 20.

“I had a mineral site set up in the woods 30 yards from my ladder stand, with a couple trail cameras nearby,” says Ferriman. “The big buck came through the area the night of Oct. 18, and I got one photo of him, and he was gone.

“The next night on Oct. 19 he came to the mineral site at 6 p.m., and he hung around awhile. The buck checked the same mineral spot three times that night, so I knew I had to hunt the stand the next evening provided I had a good northeast wind.”

Fortunately, the wind was perfect, and the crossbow hunter walked to his stand that following afternoon.

“I bumped a couple does walking 300 yards to the stand, but the place is full of deer and no matter how or when I go in I move some deer,” he says. “I got up in my stand, and pretty soon I was surrounded by about a dozen does.

“They were very close, and I’m convinced they didn’t catch my scent because of the Ozonics scent control I was using. It was 70 degrees and I was sweating a lot. But no deer scented me.”

That evening was only the second time Ferriman had hunted the spot, and he knew another heavy buck was in the vicinity, too.

“I had two big bucks in the area – I’m just glad the biggest one showed up first,  so I didn’t have to decide whether to take the smaller one, which was still a giant deer,” he says.

With does everywhere around his ladder stand, Ferriman noticed movement on a trail and quickly realized the huge non-typical buck was headed toward his mineral site.

“He came straight in toward me from 90 yards away where I first spotted him,” he says. “I almost took a shot at him at 50 yards, but he kept coming and a closer shot was what I wanted.

“He went behind a downed tree and some brush and just stood there. Then he stepped out, head down, but was facing me. I thought about a neck shot when he looked up. But just then a doe behind me made a noise, and he turned quartering away, and I took my shot at 30 yards.”

Using a Ravin crossbow, his Rage Hypodermic 2-blade, 100-grain arrow penetrated completely through the buck.

“I heard a loud thud from the arrow hitting and watched him run – and almost in slow motion – he went 50 yards and fell,” Ferriman recalls. “I was in disbelief and couldn’t comprehend how fast he’d piled up.”

Ferriman used binoculars to check the downed buck, and confirmed the giant deer was down for good.

He sent out text messages to his wife Holly and some friends alerting them of his success, and requesting help to get the deer out.

Shortly, Holly and his pals arrived and used a drag sled to get the huge buck out of the woods and into a truck. They went to a friend’s house, where they had a scale that could weigh the massive deer.

Ferriman says the deer weighed 290 pounds, not field dressed.

He took the buck to Toby Hughes, a Buckmasters official scorer in Ohio, who measured the rack’s 28 scorable points at 250 3/8s inches.

The deer is estimated at 5.5 to 6.5 years old, and its teeth will be officially aged, just as Ferriman does with all his bucks.

Read Next: Ohio Farmer Tags 231-Inch ‘Flyer’ Buck That He Missed Two Years Ago

Ferriman is a schooled taxidermist and will have the deer mounted, perhaps even a full-body mount.

“I’ve shot some great deer, some up to 150-inches,” he says. “But this buck is far and away the best I’ve ever taken.”

#8379. The Future Wild

In Spain’s emptying countryside, nature is moving back in.

The first thing you notice in an abandoned Spanish village is the swallows.

Outside, they swoop zestfully up and down in wavy crests and troughs, cutting through the air, darting through broken windows and front doors at reckless speed, slipping through holes in the masonry with astonishing precision, and alighting, casually, in their chosen nests. It’s as if they know every corner of the building. It’s as if they own the place.

And they do. There’s no one else here. By some estimates, Spain has more than three thousand abandoned villages. I was in one called Las Casillas de Bezas, in the eastern half of the country, in the province of Teruel, high-stepping over brambles, ducking as swallows darted around my head, and wondering if I was striding into the ancient past or the deep future.

I was on the trail of abandonment, particularly what follows when humans leave the countryside, which is happening not just in Spain, but across Europe, and

#8378. It Took Six People and a Tractor to Haul This Massive Black Bear Off the Mountain

Published Oct 29, 2026 9:29 AM EDT

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Cecil Jackson, age 69, climbed into his elevated Millennium platform hunting blind the afternoon of October 24. It was opening day of archery bear season in this area of the Appalachian Mountains in southeast Kentucky. Jackson didn’t know it at the time, but he was about to take one of the biggest black bears in the area.

Archery deer season was also open and Jackson was going to take whatever the mountain provided.

“I was hunting deer or bear, whatever came along,” the just-retired Kentucky Utilities worker from the town of Pineville tells Outdoor Life. “I had trail cameras set up and I knew there were a few bears in the area. But I never imagined shooting a bear, because I had no gun with me in case I shot one and had to track it.”

Jackson’s blind was situated on rolling private farmland, and late that afternoon a fawn deer strolled down a mountain trail toward Jackson shortly before nightfall.

“It stood there awhile, then snapped its head up and looked up the mountain trail where it had come from,” Jackson says. “Then the deer left the area running. I thought maybe a buck was coming, but about 30 yards away a bear showed up.”

“That bear looked at me, turned to head after where the fawn had run, and that’s when I shot him with my Ravin crossbow,” Jackson says. “The bear ran about 100 yards, then turned into a thicket and I never saw or heard it again.”

The veteran hunter knew he’d made a good shot on the bear. He waited about 10 minutes in his blind, then went out and found his arrow, but there wasn’t much of a blood trail.

“Without a gun I wasn’t gonna track that bear alone,” he says. “That’s when a friend of mine called me and I told him I’d shot a bear, and I asked if he had a pistol with him.”

His buddy Tanner Jackson (no relation to Cecil) said he did have a gun and shortly met Cecil to start tracking the bear that night.

“I’m colorblind and have a tough time on a blood trail,” Cecil says. “We had a light, but it was a hard go trailing that bear.”

After about 70 yards of following faint blood sign, they stopped and used a high beam flashlight to scan the woods.

“I told Tanner to keep that pistol of his handy, and about that time I spotted the bear lying just off the woods path,” Cecil says. “I tossed a stick at it, but it didn’t move so we figured it was dead. When we walked up to it we couldn’t believe how big it was. We tried to lift just its head up but couldn’t.”

They phoned a nearby farm neighbor and some more friends. Using country woods savvy and a low spot in the road, they rigged a rope on a block and loaded the bear onto the tailgate of Jackson’s truck. They were just able to manhandle the whole bear into their truck.

“I didn’t think we could get that truck up and away from the low road spot, but that old truck in 4-wheel drive made it,” Cecil says. “It took six adults and a tractor to finally get that bear off the mountain.”

The hunters didn’t get the bear home until 11 p.m. that night.

The following day, James Dixon from the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources checked Cecil’s huge bear, which field dressed at an estimated weight of over 500 pounds. The bear measured 105-inches (nearly 9 feet) from nose to tail. Its neck measured 33 inches in circumference.

“James said he’d not seen a bear that size and believed it was the heaviest one taken so far from Kentucky this year – its huge head may be big enough for a record,” Cecil says. “I’m not much for bear meat, but some friends are, and I gave it all to them.

“I also gave away its fur to a buddy. But I may keep its skull for a European mount – especially if the head is of record size.”

#8377. Review: Mountain Equipment Switch Base Zip T

The Mountain Equipment Switch Base Zip T is an ultralight, close-fitting base layer designed for high-output cold-weather activities. It is made with Octa Fleece, a warm, highly breathable ultralight fleece similar to Polartec Alpha Direct, but much more durable, and pairs well with a windbreaker or winter shell jacket.

If you’re not familiar with Mountain Equipment, they’re a highly regarded British manufacturer that has designed technical outdoor gear for mountaineering and polar exploration since 1961. They make a wide range of products, including technical clothing, sleeping bags, and mountaineering backpacks. Backcountry.com carries their products in the United States. I’ve been recommending Mountain Equipment’s men’s Ibex and women’s Chamois softshell pants for winter hiking for years, and they’re still best in class.

The top uses 20-denier, 100% Octa Fleece, made from a specialized hollow polyester fiber with eight radial projections that give the yarn a gear- or octopus-like cross-section. The hollow center and projecting “fins” create insulating air spaces that trap warm air, letting water vapor escape. Octa Fleece has a similar warmth-to-weight ratio as Polartec Alpha Direct but is more durable, which is why larger clothing manufacturers such as Arc’teryx and Mountain Hardwear use it and are developing products with it. See our FAQ for a more detailed comparison of Octa Fleece and Polartec Alpha Direct.

The inside of the Switch Base Zip-T is a fuzzy, warm fabric that is a delight to wear next to the skin or over a thin base layer, while the outer surface is made of highly breathable, abrasion-resistant mesh.

The Switch Base Zip-T can be worn as a base layer or a mid-layer over a thin base. The interior has a fuzzy fleece texture that feels warm and comfortable. Flatlocked seams improve next-to-skin comfort by reducing bulk and minimizing potential irritation. The exterior is an open and breathable mesh that is much more abrasion-resistant. Thumbhole loops help keep the sleeves in place when adding a midlayer or waterproof shell.

Nylon shoulder overlays protect an area that sees regular friction from backpack straps.  This added reinforcement improves the top’s suitability for regular mountain use without significantly compromising its lightweight design.

A deep half-zip provides practical ventilation when body heat builds, making the Switch Base Zip T more adaptable than a standard crew-neck baselayer. Similarly, the loose wrists let you pull the sleeves up your arms to vent more heat. I’ve found the Switch to be a delightful base and mid-layer, worn by itself or under a windbreaker on a chilly morning. The fabric is more wind-resistant than a mid-layer hoodie made with Polartec Alpha Direct, and I like using a pullover like it in winter more than a hoodie because it’s easier to layer with the shells and headgear (hats) I typically wear.

The Switch Base Zip T is designed for a wide range of cold-weather activities, including:

It performs best during activities that involve frequent changes in effort and temperature since you can vent it so easily or layer it with a windbreaker or shell to increase wind resistance and heat retention. It also delivers warmth well above its weight, making it a lightweight midlayer that packs an outsized amount of warmth.

The Mountain Equipment Switch Base Zip T is a well-designed cold-weather or winter base layer for active users who prioritize low weight, quick drying, and effective ventilation. Its Octa Fleec fabric provides lightweight warmth while helping manage moisture, and the half-zip makes it easy to regulate temperature during demanding climbs and ski tours. It is not the best choice for maximum insulation when activity levels are low, but that is not its main purpose. For fast-moving winter adventures, the combination of comfortable seams, reinforced shoulders, and quick-drying performance makes the Switch Base Zip T a strong and practical choice.

Disclosure: Mountain Equipment donated a garment for review.
