#8335. One Wrong Move Could Be Fatal. So Why Are These Climbers Competing at Free Soloing?

Michael Reese at the top of the First Flatiron in Boulder, Colorado (Photo: Courtesy of Michael Reese)

About our reporting: Climbing reporter Holly Chen interviewed three free soloists and one additional speed climber in Boulder, researched fatalities in Accidents in North American Climbing, and pulled from her own experience free soloing the Second Flatiron to answer questions about the world of competitive free soloing.

I stood waiting in front of a health food restaurant in south Boulder, Colorado. The Flatirons rose high above the building, their slabs of red sandstone jutting out of the mountainside like the spines of a prehistoric monster.

On September 3, 32-year-old climber Michael Reese broke the First Flatiron’s fastest known time (FKT) from the dirt at its base to the summit anchor, with no rope. He climbed the Direct Route (5.6,R; 1,000ft) of the East Face in 7 minutes 51 seconds, breaking what he believed would be the last minute barrier of this generation. The previous record was 8 minutes 33 seconds, set by Joe Kennedy in 2022.

Which one is Michael Reese? Everywhere I looked at the restaurant, less than a 10 minute drive from the Chautauqua trailhead, I saw La Sportiva and Scarpa running shoes, Salomon running vests, and folded ultralight running poles sticking out of ultralight backpacks. Any of these people could have just come off the climb.

The ease was the first thing I noticed about Reese. For someone who holds multiple FKTs in the Flatirons and one on Yellow Spur (5.8; 550ft) in Eldorado Canyon, I expected him to be cocky, confident, maybe a little elitist; he was anything but. Reese smiled easily, laughed easily, and spoke candidly, unperturbed by the recorder sitting between us. He was leaving for Yosemite the following day, and we exchanged stories of our experiences climbing in the Valley. When I joked about my personal best up the First Flatiron–somewhere shy of an hour, although I did not officially keep time–he congratulated me genuinely.

“You can do it,” Reese urged. “Get some racing shoes. Do some warmups … You’ll be going faster.”

As climbing has grown, it has increasingly legendized free soloing and going fast—but we’ve rarely seen these two disciplines combined and going without a rope. The Oscar-winning film Free Solo (2017) made the term so mainstream that it recently appeared in a Taylor Swift song, and speed climbing records have made headlines again and again. But these fantastical feats of risk and speed are usually in the hands of highly experienced climbers, such as Alex Honnold, the spectacular pendulum of Dean Potter, or Yosemite Search and Rescue members. Additionally, most of these races happen on cliffs that the average person can’t easily ascend, such as El Capitan.

Reese is a different kind of figure. A Boulder local, he is not sponsored, and not a professional. Reese started climbing at the University of Colorado (CU) Boulder in 2014. The first time he went up the First Flatiron, he said to himself, “If I get off this [alive], I’m never climbing again.” And the First Flatiron is far from inaccessible; with the base a 1.3-mile hike from the trailhead, for many people, the barrier to entry is only a pair of shoes.

The new FKT leaves me with an uneasy mix of admiration and doubt. A person’s risk is not entirely his own when he takes it in a busy place like Chautauqua Park, where hikers, runners, picnickers, and climbers share the same space. So is competitive free soloing on low fifth-class terrain something to celebrate or a toxic addiction to discourage? A fatal fall is always possible, and the barrier to entry is so low. In fact, anyone writing about it, including myself, is working on blurry ground where reporting and the glorification of risk are hard to tell apart. Does this recognition create a feedback loop that incentivizes more to partake in the risky sport?

To understand how competitive free soloing actually operates, I had to go back to the people who have been going fast on this rock for decades before Reese.

The history of speed records in the Flatirons runs through a small, unusual club called The Satan’s Minions Scrambling Club, which Bill Wright started in 2001. Three of its members told me they don’t “race” each other. Instead, they have “personal time trials,” to avoid the ire of the Parks & Open Space regulations, which prohibit races.

The club keeps books. Stefan Griebel, a longtime member, whom a mutual friend described to me as someone who holds “every record under the sun,” has a meticulously kept log book detailing every FKT on a Flatiron dating back to the 1980s. Today, members’ times are verified by Strava entries.

Griebel met Wright in 2003 and joined the club’s annual Flatiron scrambles, which have now run for about 22 years. Each one starts at a trailhead, free solos a Flatiron, and ends back in the parking lot. Buzz Burrell, a trail-running legend then 52, reset the trailhead-to-trailhead mark at 35 minutes and change. Griebel, who was half Burrell’s age at the time, couldn’t keep pace.

“[Buzz] just dropped every single person that day,” Griebel reminisced.

A year later, trail runner Dave Mackey took Burell’s trailhead-to-trailhead FKT down to 33:19. But being a trail runner, Griebel knew he would have the upper hand on rock. In 2010, Griebel closed the gap, and took the record to 33:05. The record changed hands to Mathias Messner in 2015 and Kyle Richardson in 2019.

In the spring of 2020, Reese returned to Boulder from a biotech master’s program at California Polytechnic State University. The COVID pandemic had canceled the triathlon nationals he’d spent months training for, and he had a season of fitness and nothing to spend it on. He decided to see how fast he could go on the Flatirons. It began as a text-message rivalry with Joe Mitchem, a friend from CU’s cross-country team, over Freeway (5.0; 600ft) on the Second Flatiron. Reese didn’t have Strava and didn’t know the records existed until the two of them realized they’d gone under the standing Freeway mark of about 6:20. That fall, he entered the club’s time trials and finished second.

Griebel remembers meeting Reese on the First Flatiron. The two soloed to the summit and trotted down together. “He can run uphill like nobody I’ve ever seen,” Griebel said.

The base-to-summit FKT, the one Reese prefers, was still Griebel’s in 2020, at 9:25. Reese told me the time stunned him. That summer, Reese broke it by seconds. Then Joe Kennedy, a California athlete, broke that in 2022 to 8:33. That sent Reese into harder training than he’d done in 2020 or 2021, and this September brought the record down to 7:51.

The club looks different today. It is still heavily male dominated; Griebel estimates eight men for every one woman participant. And membership is less casual. “We have some entrance requirements now,” Griebel said. “We don’t want to invite people into the club that aren’t okay with the risk and that are also very solid, obviously, on the rock.”

What the club shows is a culture more wary than toxic. It vets its members, keeps careful books, and wants to stay on good terms with the land managers. It also shows a feedback loop; each record pulled in the next challenger. Reese told me every broken record “ingrains it more as something to go for.” He felt inspired when he learned of Griebel’s record. Camaraderie and friendly competition keep people incentivized and returning. But this wariness only goes so far; while the Satan’s Minions can vet their members, they can’t actually stop others from trying competitive free soloing, too.

Reese said he has now climbed the First Flatiron 800 times. It taught him that the risk “is never zero,” but he believes it to be smaller than most people imagine.

Even inside the scene, no one agrees on what speed does to the odds of surviving a free solo. Griebel says that when he’s pushing hard, heart pounding and moving upward, he’s “less likely to make a mistake.” Kate Kelleghan, who holds the women’s Naked Edge (5.11b; 460ft) record with Laura Pineau, says free soloing only makes up about one percent of her climbing. “This is super high risk and low reward,” she told me. “I’ve always felt way safer and stronger on a rope.” John Alcorn, who holds the Diamond speed record, free soloing Casual Route (5.10a; 900ft), says going fast piles more risk onto something already dangerous. “You get one shot,” he told me, “and if you blow it, you’re dead.”

In his trip report, Alcorn wrote, “I accept the position that climbing without a rope is a pretty dumb thing to do, and I believe that it shouldn’t be glorified, normalized, or encouraged in any way.” When a friend’s wife called it “incredibly stupid” over dinner, he agreed.

Alcorn said the FKTs are “extremely competitive. We’re essentially all competing with each other. But all these guys are my friends.” He admitted that if someone took his Diamond time by a minute or two, “Oh, I’d be pissed.” Then he caught himself: “That’s just pure ego … one of the worst reasons to climb without a rope.”

According to Accidents in North American Climbing, there have been six fatalities in the Flatirons since 2016. All of them involved free soloists, although none of them involved speed climbers. That number puts the danger in soloing, not the speed.

Low fifth-class terrain pulls in runners, a demographic far larger than climbing. “The accessible, low-angle slabs of the Flatirons frequently lure inexperienced or ill-prepared scramblers,” wrote the ANAC editors in 2017.

Reese has noticed more crossover of hybrid athletes; people coming from a very high level running background. Alcorn saw the same shift from the trail running side: As running records multiply, people are “diversifying what counts as a goal,” and he finds it hard to say where running and scrambling stop and climbing begins. Griebel says the overlap between strong runners and people comfortable soloing is thin, and that overlap is the only reason he has ever held a record.

This summer Reese found a 20-year-old about 100 feet up at dusk, shaking, with no headlamp, his feet slipping. Reese guided him down a gully. By the time they reached the ground, it was too dark to see his own outstretched hand.

I have felt that same dread myself. In the summer of 2025, I took out-of-town friends up on a free solo of the second Flatiron. Near the top, three college-aged men were climbing without a rope, one in climbing shoes and two in running shoes. The leader, about fifteen feet above me, was shaking badly. I waved my friends to the left, afraid that if he fell, we would be in his path.

But inexperienced climbers aren’t always the ones to watch. In 2020, a man fell to his death on Freeway, even after he reportedly had climbed it “hundreds of times.”

The scrambling club’s precautions don’t reach the people who get in trouble because those people aren’t in the club. And just because one is solid on rock doesn’t mean they’ll never fall. Its members can be practiced and clear-eyed about the risk, but the rock belongs to everyone. “They don’t do it because they see somebody going fast,” said Griebel, referring to inexperienced scramblers. “They just see somebody soloing.”

The stereotype is that this is a content game. Climbers like Lincoln Knowles, who posts his free solos to a large and young following, make the impression that free soloing is about social media fame and monetization.

The record-holders I talked to disagree. Reese began timing himself in 2020 without Strava, unaware the records existed. “If there was no social media, no recognition of any kind, would you still do it?” I asked Reese. The answer was an unequivocal yes. “I’m more interested in doing the actual thing than the broadcasting of what I’ve done,” Reese said.

Alcorn never posted his Diamond record, a choice he called intentional. “I just don’t even want ego in the loop,” he said. Griebel’s Instagram account is private except to close friends. Reese’s posts reads more like a logbook than a boast.

Still, the pull of recognition isn’t zero. Reese allows that recognition probably motivates him now that it exists, but he still climbs for himself and not a like button. Alcorn admits that without a culture of records he probably wouldn’t have tried the Diamond record. Kelleghan sits in the middle. She has a following and has been paid, including for a watch ad, but says she has never climbed something just to post it.

Whatever these climbers are after, audiences both on and offline take their own lessons from the best in the sport.

On the Flatirons, free soloing and speed have become synonymous; on the Naked Edge, a short drive south, they still sit apart, for now. Some Boulder climbers are free soloing the Naked Edge already, Kelleghan said, and she knows at least one who has soloed it quickly, though not for a record. This climber, who Kelleghan refuses to name, believes the speed record will eventually belong to a free soloist. Kelleghan disagrees. A free soloist can’t push as hard, she argued, because “if you’re simul climbing, if you fall, it would be unpleasant, but you wouldn’t die.”

The people I spoke with showed that records have a way of recruiting. If someone does set a free solo speed record on the Naked Edge, will it stay an outlier, or become the standard, the way that free solo ascents became the standard on the Flatirons? Kelleghan is betting against it.

So for most people who hold these records, it isn’t a content game. But a motive doesn’t have to be public or monetized to be contagious. Each time a record falls, it tells the next climber what is possible. The risk the last person accepted becomes the new baseline.

For all the attention these records draw, free soloing mostly regulates itself. Most people look at the First Flatiron and never think of climbing it, let alone without a rope. Alcorn points to an innate fear of falling “baked into us” and doesn’t expect the number of people doing this to explode just because a few records have been broken.

Some people chase records, but does that make this a toxic culture? From what I saw, it doesn’t. The record-holders I met were generous rivals, wary of their own egos, more interested in doing the thing than in being seen doing it. But “not toxic” isn’t the same as “not influential.” We are not solitary creatures, we have family and friends who love us, so a risk taken is never entirely one’s own.

Reese was as easy at the end of our conversation as at the start. By the end of our meal, I had decided we were friends, so as we said goodbye, an uneasy feeling settled in my stomach.

Walking to my car, I looked up at the Flatirons. A friend of mine, Bailee Mulholland, still holds the female trailhead-to-trailhead speed record on the First. She belonged to the same scrambling club Reese does now. In 2023, she died free soloing a 5.4 route on Ypsilon Mountain (13,520ft) a few hours north. I remembered Mulholland’s unwavering bubbly personality; she smiled easily and laughed easily, too.

I don’t think the scene she came from is toxic. But I know what losing her did to the people who loved her. The risk may belong to the one who takes it. The grief never does.

#8333. Class 4 Terrain, Cozy Huts, Cold Beer: The Northern Alps Are Japan’s Best-Kept Secret

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Author and photographer Andy Cochrane spent months crafting this route from home in Bend, Oregon, consulting with multiple Japanese mountain guides, before flying to Tokyo to bring it to life. Along with four others, he ran this 100-mile technical traverse across the Northern Alps in a week, staying at mountain huts and soaking in Japanese hospitality along the way.

It’s not often that a local guide recommends helmets for a hut-to-hut trail running trip, but it’s always a sign of a good adventure if you ask me.

A couple of months before flying across the Pacific to Japan, I was on a mid-afternoon Zoom call—my third such conversation of the week—when my jaw hit the floor. I was meeting virtually with guides in the Northern Alps to learn more about the trails and huts of the range, hoping to suss out if a line I had plotted on a map was actually a feasible endeavor to run.

At the time, I wasn’t sure if anyone had run the route before us. There certainly weren’t any blogs, articles, or posts I could find about it. Hut owners on the trip later confirmed my suspicion that our 100-mile, seven-day itinerary was pretty far out of the box. Connecting the outdoor hub of Kamikochi at the southern end of the range to the Sea of Japan in the north along a single ridge line was an unheard of idea to everyone we spoke with. That made it a lot more exciting—and far from certain it would work out. If it did, however, we would get to experience all that the Northern Alps had to offer in a single push.

Because the route required a mix of trail running, boulder hopping, ladder climbing, and Class 4 scrambling, our local guide Tatsuro was adamant that we bring helmets, even if their use wouldn’t be required every day. TL;DR: he was right.

Before I get into specifics of the route and experience, let’s set the scene. The Northern Alps, or Hida Mountains, are Japan’s most primal terrain. Although lesser-known than the mountain ranges of Europe, South America, or mainland Asia, the Northern Alps are just as technical and challenging, if not more so. The range is a jagged, granite spine that defies the country’s reputation for manicured serenity. Trails in the Hida are riddled with boulders, ladders, roots, scrambling, and thick brush. Located just a few dozen miles off the Sea of Japan, the weather is incredibly fickle in the Hida, too.

Geographically, the Northern Alps lie just a few hours drive west of Tokyo on the main island and stretch across Nagano, Toyama, Gifu, and Niigata prefectures. Most of the range is inside Chubu-Sangaku National Park, which protects around 670 square miles from being absorbed by the urban centers that surround it. The Hida are widely regarded as Japan’s premier alpine terrain and feature the country’s most developed hut system, Yamagoya. These staffed huts offer hot meals, sleeping mats, water, snacks, and beer, allowing for multi-day runs and traverses with lightweight packs sans camping gear—perfect for a trip like ours.

Three years ago I ran across the Southern Alps on an ancient postal route called Nakasendo. While the Southern and Northern Alps offer remarkably different terrain and technicality, my first trip taught me much about Japanese culture and logistics that was helpful while preparing for my return.

Perhaps my biggest takeaway from that initial experience was that the language barrier is a major challenge—especially in rural places, where many people don’t speak a lick of English. While apps like Google Translate can help to order a quick meal or get assistance with navigation in a pinch, planning a trip and booking mountain huts requires someone not only fluent in Japanese, but who also understands the mountain culture. For us, that liaison was Kota.

I was connected with Kota at Japan Adventures Co. through a friend, and I honestly can’t say enough good things about him. He is an incredibly organized planner, a great communicator, and an avid hiker and trail runner. He even helped negotiate our stay with a few huts that didn’t believe our route was possible, ensuring the entire trip ran smoothly. Kota and his team lead a variety of hiking, food, and cultural trips around Japan, and are currently rolling out new trail running itineraries in the Northern Alps and elsewhere.

With help from Kota and advice from guides like Tatsuro and Paul from Nagano Adventures, I was able to refine our route to stay at unique huts, run the best trails, and find a balance between challenging and doable for each day. It’s important to note that mountain huts in Japan are warm and welcoming, but they run on rigid schedules. Breakfast is typically at 5 a.m. and dinner is around 5 p.m. If you don’t check in by 4 p.m., they will notify search and rescue, so it’s important to start early and keep an eye on your pace throughout the day.

My goal was to start in Kamikochi and end at the Seas of Japan, creating a single linkup by connecting a number of popular two- and three-day hiking routes—the Panorama Ginza Route, Mount Yari, Ura Ginza Panorama Route, the ridgeline from Mount Eboshi and Funakubo-dake, the Hachimine Kiretto, the Kaerazu no Ken (ridge of no return), and Tsugami Shindo. It’s a mouthful to say, but when drawn on a map, the routes piece together nicely, forming a (mostly) straight line running from north to south.

Getting to and from the Northern Alps isn’t terribly difficult. After landing in Tokyo (either HND or NRT), a bullet train, or Shinkansen, will take you to Matsumoto in just a few hours. From there you can take a smaller train, bus, or taxi into the mountains to begin your adventure. Returning to Tokyo is just as easy by hopping on a bullet train in a coastal city like Toyama. There are plenty of stations to choose from and you usually can find seats just a day or two in advance.

There are a few ways to shuttle your luggage from the start to the finish, but I recommend Yamato Transport. Other options include dropping bags at the post office, the front desk if you’re staying in a hotel, or even convenience stores like Lawson’s or 7-Eleven. Though this might seem risky at face value, it worked flawlessly for us. We walked into a convenience store around 10 p.m., spent a meager ten minutes filling out the paperwork, and walked out. Our bags arrived at our final hotel just after we arrived seven days later.

Despite plenty of challenges, the trip ran as smoothly as I could have imagined. We dealt with heavy rain, 50 mph winds, and thick mist for our first few days, which forced us to slow down on the scrambling sections, layer up to stay warm, and take plenty of breaks in huts along the way. Some days had tons of vert (often more than 1,000 feet per mile) and rocky trails that made running difficult, so we embraced the shuffle. On day four, when covering our most remote section, we didn’t see a single other person. Fortunately the trails are well marked, even where they are less frequented and overgrown.

The crux of the route, the Kaerazu no Ken, is a long and serpentine downclimb on Class 4 granite slabs, offering a chain for protection in some areas while others did not. This was one of the dozen or so sections that having a helmet was a welcomed addition to our kits. For those comfortable with alpine climbing, this will feel like a fun change of pace. For those afraid of exposure, it’ll be challenging. The huts themselves vary considerably from small ridgetop outposts like Funakubo to much larger and busier outfits like Hakuba Sanso. Regardless of size, every hut owner we met was incredibly kind. Japanese hospitality is something they take very seriously.

Overall, our experience in the Hida was more than we could have asked for. Steep and technical trails, unique and cozy huts, fickle yet fruitful weather, and no other Americans or Europeans along the way. It’s an undiscovered gem for anyone outside Japan. With the help of Kota, Tatsuro, and others, I’m already planning a return trip next year.

One of the lightest climbing helmets on the market, the Vapor was perfect for our trip. We frequently had sections of running between scrambles and wouldn’t leave it on because it breathes so well. The Vapor fits over a hat and under a rain jacket hood, making it great for wet days, too.

The latest from Garmin is designed for routes like ours with a solar-powered display that ran the full week on a single charge. The maps were critical on wet days when I didn’t want to use my phone, and the flashlight was perfect for early mornings trying to not wake up other guests.

The perfect size pack for a trip like ours, the Adventure was able to carry everything we needed—spare clothes, first aid, snacks, camera, and ditty—with ease, plus poles, flasks, and a phone in the external pockets. It can be adjusted on the fly to reduce bounce and chafing.

On a week-long trip you end up eating a ton of snacks—gummies, chips, gels, and whatever you can buy at the huts—but nothing hit home like GU stroops. Whether it was with morning tea, on the top of a big climb, or preventing a bonk, stroops played a big role in our success.

With major improvements from the previous version, the Speedgoat 7 was the perfect shoe for this trip, offering plenty of grip on technical scrambles and ladders, a comfortable and cushy ride for the long days, and a lay-flat tongue that kept most rocks and dirt out.

The perfect mid-layer for cool mornings or windy days, the Dawner breathes well and is quite comfortable next to skin. The exterior is stretchy and durable, which is great for running through brush and rubbing against rocks— an inevitability in terrain like the Northern Alps.

#8332. At This Resort, The Owner is Driving A Snowcat, Turning Wrenches, and Fixing Broken Fences

I’d never ridden a ski lift with the person who owns the mountain below us before, so I’m not sure if this is common.

But as we chugged from the Ski Santa Fe’s base toward its 11,075-foot peak, Ben Abruzzo noted a chairlift returning to the base that sounded squeaky, a groomer that needed tending, and an orange safety fence that had fallen over. Abruzzo—whose day was charged with showing this writer around the mountain his family has owned since the mid-1980s—interrupted his responses to any of my questions on more than a few occasions, apologizing before speaking into a small walkie-talkie mounted on his chest. He instructed this person or that to address the various tiny issues that must pop up a million times a day on a mountain, acting more like a manager than The Guy Who Owns the Mountain.

Over the course of a single lift ride, it became clear how much Abruzzo not only cared about the experience of the roughly 250,000 visitors who enjoy his family’s mountain every year but also about the mountain itself. It makes sense once you realize that Ski Santa Fe is, in a way, woven into the very fabric of the person Abruzzo is.

“It’s all I’ve ever known,” Ben said, as the lift neared Ski Santa Fe’s peak, the mountain he described as his “lifelong backyard.”

Owners and CEOs often love to say that their businesses are like a family. However, for the Abruzzos, Ski Santa Fe is not only their family business, but it’s their ancestral home.

Ben is the third-generation owner of Ski Santa Fe, following in the footsteps of his grandfather, his father, and two of his uncles, who finalized the purchase of the mountain in 1985. It was hardly a lark, as the elder Abruzzo purchased the Sandia Peak Ski Area in nearby Albuquerque in the late 1950s.

Their familial sensibility permeates much of Abruzzo’s staff. His grooming manager has worked at the mountain for thirty years. His operations manager as well. The mountain’s ticketing manager bests them both, with 32 years of service.

“I think it’s because we treat our folks right,” Abruzzo said, pointing out that when he says ‘we,’ he doesn’t just mean his father, his late grandfather, his uncles, and any other Abruzzo who’s spent time working the mountain. “Our mountain manager, our operations manager, all of our full-time staff; they’re all invested because they’re all part of this community.”

Abruzzo started working on the mountain when he was 12, at first building mountain bike trails in the summer and working in the rental shop during the season. After commissioning as an infantry officer in 2001, Abruzzo deployed to Afghanistan with the Army’s 101st Airborne Division during the height of the Global War on Terror. Abruzzo returned home in 2005, working as an area manager at Sandia Peak. He relocated to Ski Santa Fe in 2010, eventually taking over the mountain shortly before the Covid-19 pandemic.

And even though he owns the ski area, Ben still drives snowcats, still turns wrenches when chairlifts need tending. And he requires the same of all the mountain’s senior staff.

“We expect all of our managers to be well-versed in the blue-collar side of things,” he said. “And that includes me.”

Sitting high in the Sangre de Cristo Mountains, Ski Santa Fe is about a thirty-minute drive from the heart of the famously artsy city in northern New Mexico. Of course, snowy days and weekends might impact that commute time, Abruzzo admits, despite the fact that the mountain has its own dedicated road crew charged with plowing the two-lane road leading up to Ski Santa Fe. Still, as Ski Santa Fe is the only ski area in the vicinity, it’s a drive that never feels out of reach for locals and visitors alike.

In a more corporate environment, that dearth of options could provide owners an excuse to rest on their proverbial laurels. However, Abruzzo sees that scarcity as an honor to uphold. If people only have one option, it’d better be a good one.

With 88 total trails, almost evenly split across blacks, blues, and greens, a trio of terrain parks, and 1,800 feet of vertical drop, all serviced by a double lift, two triple lifts, two quad lifts, two surface lifts, and a high-speed detachable lift, the mountain is far bigger and more diverse than you might think when you hear “family-owned ski area.”

But beyond all that, Ski Santa Fe is known by locals and regulars for two main reasons: first, its off-piste skiing. And second, its snowmaking capabilities.

On the day we spent together, snow fell from the sky in big, thick flakes. It was one of the 20 or so powder days Ski Santa Fe gets each season. The tops of tall pine trees, buried in some 200 inches of snow, poked out of the thick layers of powder. It was a relatively unfamiliar sensation to this lifelong East Coaster who is far better versed in riding ice than he is powder.

Still, Abruzzo assured, even when it’s human-made, Ski Santa Fe’s snow is some of the best and most consistent there is.

“We make very dry snow,” Abruzzo said, before pointing out how the mountain’s 42 snow guns and 5-million-gallon storage tank allow them to cover most of the mountain in snow throughout the season. “It’s dry to the point where we have had snow gun companies write us a custom setting. And what you get is a much nicer surface to ski on that stays nice longer.”

A little shy of halfway down one of our day’s runs, Abruzzo cut from one groomer to another and, suddenly, a rustic, two-story shack stood surrounded by a small sea of skiers and snowboarders, each of whom seemed to have a beer, a cocktail, or a hot chocolate in hand.

At 10,500 feet, Totemoff’s sits higher than the peaks of many ski areas in North America.

And while there was no entertainment beyond some music playing over the speakers, Abruzzo assured me that Totemoff’s often plays host to live music. Above the bar, apartments for Abruzzo’s family and staff really hammer home the idea of how deeply entwined the Abruzzo family is in this mountain.

As we sat chatting over a pair of light beers, the talk eventually came back to the Abruzzo family, their lifelong marriage to this mountain. I ask Ben what it’s been like having three generations of Abruzzos run a mountain together. He quickly corrects me.

“Both of my kids work here,” he said with a laugh. “So, it’s actually four generations.”

#8331. Christopher Wren, Climber and Legendary Reporter, Had a “Wry Sense of Humor”

Christopher Wren at basecamp during the 1974 Pamir Expedition. In this photo, he is using a typewriter to draft the New York Times story that revealed the deaths of American climber Gary Ullin and eight Soviet female climbers. (Photo: Courtesy of Jed Williamson)

Christopher Sale Wren served as The New York Times bureau chief in Moscow, Cairo, Beijing, Ottawa, and Johannesburg. His creative life was deeply intertwined with a respect for nature, big expeditions and the many people he met on assignment. He passed at his home in Vermont on February 15, 2026, at age 89.

Wren began climbing as a student at Dartmouth, where he sometimes felt out of place, according to his daughter, Celia. A scholarship student whose parents were actors, he had little interest in fraternity life. In the outdoors, he found a bigger sense of kinship. He learned to climb with the college’s mountaineering club, practicing on campus at Bartlett Tower and on the nearby cliffs of Orford and Owl’s Head. According to Samuel C. Silverstein’s memorial in The American Alpine Journal, he once ended a public-speaking assignment on mountaineering by rappelling out of the classroom’s third-floor window.

In 1962, Wren joined the six-man team that made the first ascent of Denali’s Southeast Spur (Alaska grade 4, 65-degree ice). The expedition became the subject of his first major article for Look magazine, merging his climbing with his reporting into a career he chased around the world.

Twelve years later, while stationed in Moscow for the Times, he joined an American expedition to the Pamirs. On Lenin Peak (23,406ft), Wren and fellow climbers Jock Glidden and Allen Steck encountered members of a Soviet women’s team who had died in a storm. His reporting brought their tragedy to the Times front page, breaking the news of deaths Soviet authorities had kept secret.

For Jed Williamson, who was also on the Pamirs expedition, Wren’s contribution to mountaineering extended to his ability to tell its stories. “What he really brought to the mountaineering scene was his ability to write about it and put it out there,” Williamson said. “He had a really good sense of humor. He could turn a situation that one might not think was so humorous into one that was humorous.”

Even when faced with tragedy, Wren found a way to bring levity to dangerous moments. Celia remembered one story her father told about provisioning the Pamirs expedition. The American climbers wanted peanut butter, which he couldn’t find in Soviet shops. Instead, he packed tins of caviar for protein. “His teammates thought it was disgusting,” she remembers. “But he was a Renaissance man with an incredible sense of humor.”

Wren played guitar and banjo and wrote songs, two of which Johnny Cash recorded: Jesus Was a Carpenter and Gospel Road. “It was a fun thing that he did, and he was good at it,” Williamson said. “But he was never a chest pounder about that kind of thing.”

At home, Wren’s appetite for being outside became part of family life. During the family’s years in the Soviet Union, Celia remembered her father heading out on skis, pulling her and her brother behind him on a sled. He penned numerous books, from a biography of Johnny Cash to Walking to Vermont, an account of his roughly 400-mile walk home from Manhattan after retiring from The New York Times.

Williamson remembers that despite the breadth of his traveling and range of his accomplishments, Wren was down-to-earth.  “He wasn’t aloof or standoffish or anything like that,” he said. “He was happy to share.”

Late into retirement, he continued to ski and ride his mountain bike around the nearby lake. Celia remembered his ability to keep moving ahead. When recalling difficult experiences, he would often say, “Well, you know, that’s all behind us now.”

#8329. Survive Unexpected Winter Storms on the Trail With These 5 Expert Tips

Hiker on snowy path (Photo: Paul Biris / Moment via Getty)

The best way to survive a winter storm is to not get caught in one. True as that may be, however, it’s not a very useful tip when the snow has already started falling. As weather grows more unpredictable, getting stuck on the trail, even when you’ve dutifully checked the forecasts, could happen to any of us. The key to surviving is always being prepared for the worst by packing the 10 essentials and reading articles like this, even if you’re just planning to go on a day hike.

“If you ask me what’s the highest risk, it’s those short hikes because they’re the ones most people aren’t prepared for the longer term,” says Dan Wowak of Coalcracker Bushcraft, a wilderness school and YouTube channel based in Pennsylvania. “A two-mile hike can turn into a devastating emergency situation. You roll an ankle, a storm comes in, it gets dark, you have no equipment, and you don’t know what to do.”

We talked to Wowak and two other experienced hikers about what to do when bad weather rolls in with no warning. The first step: They all suggest packing the right things for winter, including an emergency shelter, communication device, extra layers, navigation, and a fire starter.

You might think that if you’re only a mile from the trailhead, you’re home free. But as snow starts to cover the trail and any tracks you may have left, you might as well be days away. “When you’re out and the weather is turning, you might be inclined to go faster,” says Danny Giovale, the founder of Kahtoola. “I would strongly suggest stopping for a sec.”

Knowing when to stop and wait out the storm will save you from precarious situations. Giovale and Wowak suggest considering how far you have left to go and the time of day. If the storm is moving in quickly and it’s getting dark, it’s best to stop and prioritize survival. Nighttime, Wowak says, is one of the worst times to travel because both visibility and temperatures are at their lowest. So if dusk approaches and you’re not prepared with the equipment and knowledge to travel in the dark, settle in to spend the night out there.

If you packed an emergency bivy or a tent, it’s crucial to set that up immediately to protect yourself from the elements, like snow, rain, and wind. Blocking the weather is going to prolong your survival timeline. “If you’re not dry, you’re in trouble really fast,” says Jon King, who hikes daily and sends the trail report for 10,000-footer San Jacinto Peak in California.

If you don’t have shelter, Giovale suggests looking for a cave or building your own in the snow. This, of course, requires prior knowledge, but the idea is to create a big pile of snow. Let it set up into a dome and then dig out a space for your body. Don’t forget to poke an air vent.

Then there are trails with man-made shelters, like on San Jacinto Peak, says King. Part of your preparation is knowing where these huts and structures are located in case you ever need them.

As your hands grow cold, they become less functional. As your body loses heat, you become at risk for developing hypothermia and making rash decisions. In addition to a shelter, Giovale always brings a lightweight shell jacket with a hood. It’s “one of the ounce-per-ounce most impactful pieces of gear,” he says. Staying as dry as possible with extra layers will keep you warm. Keep exercising and moving to stimulate blood flow to your fingers and toes.

Wowak also recommends building a fire. “Getting a campfire started is a very relaxing and primal thing that makes people feel safe in just about any situation,” he says. Some caveats apply. It’s harder to do in a torrential downpour than in a snowstorm. It’s also not always advised in fire-prone areas or during a fire ban unless it’s a life-or-death situation.

Should you spend the night outside, make sure to insulate your body from the ground so you don’t lose body heat, he adds. A foam mat will work, but in lieu of that, so will pine boughs. In a pinch, you can sit on your backpack.

Ration your water reserves to stay hydrated, or use the campfire to melt snow and warm up a drink. Drinking cold water can drain your energy, Wowak says, so warm water is better.

Unless you brought snacks, you might start to feel hunger pangs. Hydration can help there, too. “,Even if we don’t have a lot of food, if we were only planning on a day hike and a storm comes in, and we’re stuck there, being hydrated will trick your body and you won’t feel as hungry because you’re full of fluid,” Wowak says.

The worst thing you can do in any kind of survival scenario is dwell on the situation, Wowak says. Keep your mind engaged with survival tasks like making your camp bed, boiling water, organizing your gear, moving your toes and fingers, etcetera.

Giovale says to trust your prior training to get you through the storm.

“My experience with being in serious situations outside is that whatever you have learned or been exposed to, you’ll probably remember,” he says.

#8328. We Need to Move Past the “Shut Up And Die Like a Man” Mentality in the Mountains

Will Gadd (left) and his friend, the late Ken Wallator. (Photo: Will Gadd)

“Shut up and die like a man!” sounds like a line from a bad action movie, but we all heard it on the radio from the paragliding competition director. The director was yelling at a terrified pilot who thought he was falling to his death. The pilot had accidentally keyed open his radio’s shoulder mic, allowing his frantic screams to be broadcast across the competition frequency.

The unfortunate pilot begging to god to not die had collapsed his wing and plummeted in front of my eyes. Twenty-one years later, the memory of this sight and soundtrack is unforgettable, and so was the director’s barking, because there was clearly no sympathy for what the pilot thought was his final, horrific ride. Miraculously, the pilot recovered his wing and flew out to land and reflect on his life choices alone.

Most pilots didn’t think the competition director’s statement was out of line for the time. Many still don’t. I see terrible parallels between flying culture and some facets of climbing’s; in alpinism especially, some see death as an attractant, or an inevitability. Over my 40 years as an alpinist and 35 as a pilot, I’ve watched climbers experience gut-wrenching trauma—then do their best to ignore it, too scared or proud to deal with the ugly, messy truth. This avoidance sends a message to younger climbers, much like the competition director’s statement so long ago: Suck it up, move on, and die with honor if things go bad.

But living with trauma doesn’t have to be that way.

When my late friend Ken Wallator was 21, he climbed Mount Belanger in the Canadian Rockies with his girlfriend Heidi. They reached the top of the difficulties, unroped, and walked along a low-angle snow ridge to the summit of the peak. But the snow ridge was actually a massive, overhanging cornice of windblown snow, and it collapsed as they stopped to take a photo. Ken somehow managed to leap to safety but Heidi fell hundreds of meters down the face.

Ken, a brave bear of a man, downclimbed the face, found Heidi somehow still alive, and started carrying her out to a distant hut. She died before they reached it.

In the aftermath of Heidi’s death, I watched Ken receive a surprising amount of blame from grieving members of the climbing community. Didn’t he know better than to walk on a cornice? Why weren’t they roped up? Ken was already wracked with guilt from the accident. When his community piled on, their condemnation lit an internal firestorm.

Thirty years later, in 2019, Ken helped me re-roof my house. He still had the strength of a bear and I watched him haul 100-pound loads of shingles up my rickety ladder. In a rare moment of emotionality, he told me how he still hadn’t gotten over Heidi’s death, or the climbing community’s blame. We talked more about trauma, and I realized only then how that day on Mount Belanger broke my friend in a way that never healed.

As two young, hungry alpinists, Ken and I didn’t know what mental “help” looked like 30 years ago, and Ken was too much a product of his culture to take it 30 years later. Despite his immense physical and mental strength, Ken died by suicide a few weeks after our talk.

More recently, Will Stanhope’s death has brought to mind this idea of “asking for help” once more. For years Stanhope had battled desperately with alcohol. He was facing various charges at the time of his death—including assault and sexual assault—while still succeeding on difficult routes as a professional climber and mountain guide.

In our last real conversation, Stanhope talked about needing to “harden up and stop letting the carnage get to me” one minute, then sobbed about the “death camp” of hard alpine climbing the next. Like Ken and me, he had lost many friends in the mountains.

“You and I [watched] our mentors and friends die, one after another, as if everyone around us was climbing their way to oblivion,” his friend Kieran Brownie wrote in an obituary. “We couldn’t return to the mountains, we couldn’t return to each other.”

Stanhope carried a heavy weight in the final months of his life, made even heavier by grief, guilt, and irreversible mistakes. After a lifetime of hard solos and even scarier roped climbs, it seemed impossible that Stanhope would ever fall off an easy 5.11. But when he did just that last April and succumbed to a head injury, to me and other friends, Stanhope’s death felt more related to the weight he carried in his head than the climb itself. His family and friends made truly profound and sometimes wrenchingly difficult efforts to help him, but, like falling, the weights of addiction and trauma develop their own momentum.

Hard drinking, hard living, and celebrating dangerous acts—usually lauded as “bold”—are hallmarks of every mountain sport I’ve ever done, from kayaking to flying to skiing to climbing. Our literature is full of stories celebrating those who climbed hard, drank hard, and died silently.

I can’t help but wonder if our literature strives to make these deaths seem somehow valiant and necessary, like dying in the mountains is a noble sacrifice rather than the tragedy it really is. The classic mountaineering texts rarely explore the trauma that comes after seeing a friend die. They barrel ever onward to the summit.

Military veterans and first responders have a trauma-treatment framework that climbers should strive to adopt. Soldiers are not considered “weak” if they are affected by bloody combat. Paramedics are not ridiculed for taking leave after responding to a grisly car wreck. These are normal human responses, and professional groups typically have protocols for helping those involved in traumatic situations. These groups have no other choice; a traumatized team simply cannot function.

Those professional protocols weren’t there for Ken, Will, that terrified pilot, or many others, including me.

When I was 19 I tried with every tool I knew to save a fellow kayaker stuck just inches from the surface in his boat. I couldn’t reach him, and he drowned in front of me as I tried to remember how to rig a better haul system. I had nightmares for years of the paddler chasing me in the dark beside that river.

Only decades later did I seek help, after a divorce and a lot of behavior I understood even less than that terrible accident. I’m lucky I survived and sought belated help. Ken and Will and many others didn’t. Many more in our community—your friends and mine—are barely standing today, carrying crippling loads. They need help putting those loads down.

The pain of trauma does not disappear with six or 600 beers. Doing dangerous climbs or flights or other high-stimulus experiences temporarily distracts from the weight, but doesn’t solve it. There is no pack heavier than one filled with trauma you can’t put down.

One of the smartest things I’ve ever heard about trauma came after we failed to resuscitate a dying man at the base of an ice climb a few years ago. A professional responder on the scene could tell I was shaken, and looked me in the eye and said, “Post traumatic stress is normal; post traumatic stress disorder is optional—if you get help. Get help.”

I see real change today, from my wife Sarah Hueniken’s Mountain Muskox foundation to the American Alpine Club’s Grief Fund, two organizations built to support mountain-trauma survivors.

But I also still see a lot of the “Shut up and die like a man” attitude, and the celebration of “bold” yet physically unimpressive climbs that are often little more than Russian Roulette. Huge, low-angle alpine routes with immense serac and avalanche hazard are not that cool, in my book. And I see many climbers who still romanticize the wrong parts of climbing, whether that’s meaningless objective hazard or the very idea of “suffering silently.”

We need to recognize that a mountain death doesn’t end with the funeral; often that’s just the start of a very long and difficult process for everyone involved. In climbing more people die on the descent after the summit than on the climb itself.

At times I’ve felt deeply angry about our outdoor tribe’s celebration of “bold” hazards, and our denial of the after-effects of engaging in high-risk sports where participants die regularly. We often celebrate the bold free solos or dangerous alpine routes where everything clicked into place. We never celebrate the dead parent who doesn’t show up for their kids’ birthdays.

But the truth is that I laughed when the paragliding competition director said his infamous line. I promised myself that if I was in that situation in the future, I’d shut up. That became my normal. Today, I hope I’d speak up on the comment, and reach out to the guy who almost died that day. Because I’ve been him, and it sucks, and I’m trying to do better.

I’m less angry today when I think about Ken, Will, or others who have left the game, and just hope that our culture continues to evolve in the same way the first responders did, and that we ultimately celebrate survival more than dying silently. We can do better, if we want to.

Finally, if, like me, you’ve been through the trauma wringer, it often takes help to sort it out. We’re not tougher than the veterans or first responders even if our culture says we “should” be—we’re just less educated about intense trauma.

The goal is to return to full function and fly in life, not get stuck in the inevitable mental dust devils of mountain death. Peace to those hurting, it can get better with help. Substances and more dangerous living may distract us short term, but long term the combo is deadly despite the romantic words we historically place on both. I write these words for the future Wills and Kens, they are me, you, our friends.

Shutting up is not a solution, because silence is death.

#8327. What Matters Most to Jimmy Chin? The Oscar-Winning Director on Fear, Parenting, and His New Book.

(Photo: National Geographic/Savannah Cummins)

When Jimmy Chin was in his twenties, living out of a 1989 Subaru Loyale somewhere between Yosemite and the Tetons, he kept trying to explain climbing to his father. His father, a librarian at Mankato State University in Minnesota, would listen, and then say: “Our language is 5,000 years old, and there is no word for what you do.”

Chin has spent the decades since building a vocabulary for it anyway, as a climber, a photographer, and the Oscar-winning director of Free Solo featuring Alex Honnold, and his latest film, Everest: The Other Side, which documents Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson’s attempt to climb and ski down the North Face of the world’s tallest mountain.

His new book, Rules to Live By (Celadon), presents other people’s words, but is also part memoir. It’s built from ten conversations with people who have lived on their own terms: Yvon Chouinard, Yo-Yo Ma, Simone Biles, Ridley Scott, Kelly Slater, Annette Bening, Lynsey Addario, Kris Tompkins, Alex Honnold, and Bill King, a retired command master chief of SEAL Team 6. He asks each of them some version of the same question: In the end, what really matters? And in the end, we learn what matters most to Jimmy Chin as well.

Earlier this month, I sat down with Chin onstage at the Bell House in Brooklyn. It was his first book event, and he confessed he hadn’t reread the book since turning it in. “There’s a reason I’m a filmmaker,” he told the crowd. “Writing is really, really difficult.” What followed covered violin practice, an undisclosed military base, and a missing sock. The conversation has been edited and condensed.

OUTSIDE: You write that you’re “the only son of an only son of an only son.” That sounds like a lot of pressure.

Jimmy Chin: I started violin when I was three, and it became two hours of practice a day. Then martial arts, two hours a day. Then homework. That was my weekdays, and it was all I knew. But I learned discipline, and there was a very high expectation for excellence. My dad always said, “If you’re going to do it, you might as well do it well.” I hated that. Sometimes I still struggle with it.

There’s a scene in the book where you’re practicing violin, staring out the window at the forest. When did the forest win?

Chin: Anytime I did well in school, my reward was running off into the woods. There were no rules out there. My parents were librarians, so I always had a lot of books, and later, when they asked how I ended up doing this, I said, “It’s your fault. You gave me all these books.” I found climbing in college, and it was the first thing that felt like a calling. Growing up, I literally thought there were three jobs: lawyer, doctor, or professor. So after graduation I told my parents I’d take one year off, get it out of my system, and then pursue my real career. Which was a total lie. From 21 to 28 I lived out of my car, or in a cave in Camp 4, or in a chicken coop in Jackson.

Chin: My sister, who went to Stanford and worked at Yale for 18 years, was my huge advocate. I’d ask her how Mom was doing, and she’d say, “Mom just keeps saying, ‘I raised a homeless man.” With my dad, I deeply wanted him to understand me. People see the films and photographs and ask about the greatest risk I’ve ever taken. It definitely wasn’t a mountain. It was being in my early twenties, full of doubt. There are a lot of storm days, sitting in a cave with water dripping, soaking wet, thinking, What am I doing here? Meanwhile your friends are going to grad school and starting careers.

And during this time, you were in a reggae band.

Chin: I dropped violin after high school and picked up the guitar. The furthest thing I could think of from a concerto in D minor was covering Bob Marley. The whole band was classically trained kids. Everybody was technically skilled, so we could play whatever we wanted.

How did you choose the ten people in the book?

Chin: My documentaries take four, five, six, seven years. You have to bleed for them. You can only make so many films in a lifetime, and there are so many people I admire who I’ll never make a film about. I wanted the book to be a constellation: totally different backgrounds, totally different careers. After these extraordinary lives, what have you discovered really matters? What did success look like when you started, and what does it look like now? I had just turned 50, so I was looking back at my life in phases and thinking about what was to come.

Chin: After Meru, producers kept asking what was next. I mentioned to my friend Evan Hayes, who became a producer on Free Solo, that I’d been thinking about a documentary about Alex. I hadn’t even finished his name before he said, “That’s it.” National Geographic green-lit it immediately. I hadn’t even made a pitch deck.

I’d been filming and photographing Alex for ten years. I’ve worked with some of the greatest adventure athletes of our time, people at the pinnacle of their sports. All of them were anomalies within their sport. In my mind, Alex was an anomaly among anomalies. Even athletes at that level were confounded by what he was doing.

So I called him: “Good news, the film’s green-lit.” He said, “Great, because I’m thinking about soloing El Cap.” I said, “No. Not making that film.” I literally called Evan and said, “I’m out. Done.”

Chin: Among his friends, none of us would even talk about that idea. We didn’t want to put it in the ether. We’d seen the trajectory. He soloed Moonlight Buttress, which was outrageous. Then he soloed Half Dome. We were talking about breaking speed records on Half Dome, not free soloing it. It wasn’t hard to see what came after that. We just didn’t want to say it out loud. And then he dropped it in my lap. My fear was obvious: What if filming him causes him to fall? That’s not something I could live with.

Chin: He was going to do it anyway. I knew Alex really well. I took him on his first international expedition, and we’d done so much together. And I trusted him. Alex was the most calculated person I’d ever met. He had instinct, he was extremely smart, and it was never about external validation. He’s also straightforward, to a fault. He’s been well trained by now, with all the awards. But when I first met him, he’d say things and we’d be like, “You can’t say that.” If he isn’t comfortable doing something, he’ll tell you, and tell you why it’s stupid.

So we moved forward, and I gave my crew three rules. They were almost all elite professional climbers, because that’s the only team you could have: a short list of people who are both. Number one, we’re his friends first. Second, we’re climbers; you think like a climber before you pull out the camera. Third, we’re filmmakers. The film’s needs can never supersede Alex’s needs.

People saw the brain scan in the film and decided Alex was superhuman. You write that he resents that.

Chin: Because it’s just not true. He says, “I feel fear. I’ve always felt fear.” One of the reasons he started soloing was that he was so shy he was too scared to ask people to climb with him. So he climbed by himself. His process was to step outside his comfort zone a little at a time, in a regimented, disciplined way, until the things that scared him were well within it. The film took almost four years. But he’d been training for that climb his entire career. We left the brain scan open to interpretation, but that’s his process.

In 2017 you were trying to dial down the risk in your life. Then Conrad Anker and Alex asked you to come to Antarctica, and you went. You argue in the book that children need parents who are alive, but also parents who feel alive inside. Is that an argument or a good excuse?

Chin: Those are really personal decisions. It’s impossible to justify to a child that their parent died in the mountains doing what I do. I don’t know if there’s a right answer. I’ve lost a lot of friends in the mountains, some of them parents. After my friend Hilaree Nelson died, Bill King wrote to me, and I wrote back: “The mountains give us so much life, yet they take so much life away. It never makes sense, but we understand.” He quoted that line in his retirement speech. So it’s not an excuse. I believe your kids want you alive physically, and alive as yourself. For better or worse, this is my calling.

How do you tell fear that’s protecting you from fear that’s psyching you out?

Chin: Fear can sharpen your senses or paralyze you. When things are going sideways, panic never serves you. So you break it down: How much of this is perceived risk, and how much is actual risk? That exercise alone brings you back into the present. You set the perceived risks aside, focus on what’s real, and mitigate it. Then you make a plan and execute.

I love how all Bill King wanted to know was why you turned around 100 meters from the summit of Meru.

Chin: I got a surprise call from SEAL Team 6 asking me to come talk at the base. They gave me a date, a time, and an airport. I got on a plane, they flew me to an undisclosed location, took my phone. I hadn’t been nervous speaking in years, but these guys roll in and size you up. Someone told me every member of Team 6 had watched Meru. When I finished, a guy in the back cut to the chase: “How did you decide to turn around 100 meters from the summit?” I knew the entire reason I was there was to answer that question. That was Bill.

When you’ve put years into an objective and it’s within sight, and things aren’t right, it takes extraordinary discipline to walk away. On Meru we had seven days of food and were on the wall for 19. We crossed so many of our own lines, deliberately. You set a line, reach it, evaluate, set another. The more you do that, the more invested you are, and the harder it is to turn around.

You and the SEALs share a no-asshole rule. Tell me about that.

Chin: I asked Bill what trait gets people through training. He didn’t flinch: “Humor.” If a guy is getting his ass handed to him and he’s still cracking jokes, they’re not worried about him. It’s the same in the mountains. Humor changes the environment and brings you back to good, rational decisions. My selection process isn’t as serious as theirs, but these are the people holding a rope for you. You can’t have people who only think about themselves. And you can feel it. In conversation, it’s “I, I, I, me.”

Yvon Chouinard is the closest thing you have to a guru. He tells you, “It’s so easy to complicate your life. It’s so much harder to simplify it.” Have you managed it?

Chin: On expeditions, yes. That’s part of why I love them: the best version of me comes out. We’re brutal about simplifying, because every ounce counts. Everything is about efficiency, even how much stress you allow, even your heart rate. I can stay really calm in the worst situations. But if I can’t find my matching sock at home, it’s all over. In the mountains, when things are going sideways, I’m like, oh, this is casual.

You have kids. Do you worry about whether the wild places you’ve spent your life in will still be there for them?

Chin: It’s what the last pages of the book are about. I think of it with Yvon on one end and Kris Tompkins on the other. They’ve both had a tremendous impact on my life, and I’ve talked with both of them about this a lot.

Yvon always says, “Everybody has different tools. Whatever tool you have in your toolbox, whatever you’re good at, that’s what you should contribute.” It’s not only activism. His example is that if you’re an accountant, there are a ton of grassroots organizations that need accountants. So you ask: What can I contribute? Contribute what you have.

Chin: Storytelling, and a platform. That’s why I made Wild Life after Free Solo. I had the chance to finance a film about conservationists, which I probably wouldn’t have had otherwise. It’s about Doug and Kris Tompkins, who preserved something like 17 million acres over a 25-year dream of creating national parks. I’ve brought my kids down there. Those are the things I hope will make a difference: telling these stories, and putting them in a book. What Yvon and Kris have to say is so much more compelling than what I have to say about it.

#8326. 4 Backcountry Field Repairs That Can Save Your Trip (When Duct Tape Isn’t Enough)

No matter how well you’ve prepared or how careful you are with your gear, at some point, whether by cactus spine or sheer volume of trail miles, you’re going to tear a piece of clothing. Or, if you’re me, you’re going to flop down on your sleeping pad, which is on top of your toiletry bag, which holds a pair of impossibly vertical tweezers, and punch an irreparable hole in your mat on the first night of a 225-mile backpacking trip.

You can’t fix every gear problem in the field—a melted down jacket is going to need professional attention or replacement—but with a few simple supplies and some know-how you can handle more of them than you think. Here are four field repairs beyond taping your down jacket you should know, along with a minimal repair kit to get you to the next road crossing.

The glue line that attaches the bottom package—the midsole and outsole—to the shoe upper is the most common structural failure in footwear. While you can manage a few days with a blown-out upper or worn-down outsole tread, the bottom of your shoe flapping in the breeze is a problem.

If you’re close enough to town or have a sense of humor, you can wear your Crocs as hiking shoes. For the rest of us, use a combination of lacing, zip ties, and duct tape to keep your kicks together long enough to get back to civilization. The most secure way to reattach the bottom of the shoe to the top is with an X pattern, similar to how you’d wrap a sprained ankle. If you have a spare set of laces or shock cord, begin at the front of the shoe and criss-cross over the bottom and top in a series of figure-eights until you reach the top of the laces. From here, you can cover the lacing with duct tape in the same pattern. If you brought zip ties, you can punch through the outsole/midsole (be sure to punch far enough in that it doesn’t wear through the side) and the edge of the upper where it won’t rub or cause blisters. Secure it tightly, then finish with the duct tape in a figure-8 pattern.

I typically don’t carry single-use items in my pack aside from the core components of my kit, but a tent pole splint is an exception. Tent poles carry high amounts of tension from taut pitches and are under even more strain in high winds, and the tape-a-stake-to-the-pole simply does not work. A tent pole splint (or sleeve) is a tube made from the same material as the pole, and simply slides over the bent or broken section to create an unbroken line.

Before you do anything else, straighten the bent pole as much as possible or line up the two broken sections as close as they can get. Once the sleeve is centered over the break, secure it with plenty of duct tape. The pole splints are typically not much wider than the pole itself, so it should hold in place fairly well until you can get a replacement pole section.

I’ve slapped plenty of patches onto my down jacket and sleeping pads, but tearing your fly is trickier because you’re relying on the material for waterproofing. I ripped a 10-inch hole in my Big Agnes Copper Spur tent a few years ago, and my attempt at a duct-tape repair held up for about six minutes before condensation separated it again. This is where the Tenacious Tape comes in handy, with its flexible nylon, vinyl, or ripstop material and aggressive adhesive backing. It sticks better than duct tape and can fend off a decent amount of moisture for a surprisingly long time.

Be sure to clean the area around the tear as thoroughly as possible (alcohol wipes come in handy here) and dry it thoroughly before applying the tape. GearAid also makes an incredibly waterproof Aquaseal adhesive compound that can act as a seam sealer or smooth on over raincoat tears.

I must be cursed with backpacking stoves, because I feel like my ignitor stops working after my first few trips. I try to remember a lighter for this very reason, but if you didn’t and the finicky ignitor stopped sparking, you can try repositioning the electrode tip. This works if you can hear the igniter clicking but not lighting the gas—the delicate metal electrode wire likely bent away from the port.

Use your multitool pliers here and position the tip five millimeters (just under 1/4 inch) from the center ring, which should be enough for the spark to jump. The wire on the popular MSR PocketRocket tends to slip out of its guide tube, and if you know what to look for, you can slide it back into the alignment sleeve to restore contact. This video demonstrates replacing the ignitor on a similar stove. (Alternatively, just remember your lighter.)

Some items, like load-bearing pack straps or buckles, will need to be tied together until you get to town, but there are a few things that are handy to take into the backcountry.

The short answer is tape, tape, tape, tape. I wrap a healthy dose of duct tape (bonus points for weird patterns) around my trekking poles or a prescription bottle to cobble together many repairs. I also bring a few inches of Tenacious Tape, designed to patch waterproof fabrics like rain jackets and tent flies, and a NoSo Patch, which works wonders for keeping the feathers inside a torn jacket or sleeping bag.

For thru-hikes or longer trips where I’m going to be way in the backcountry, I bring a tiny sewing kit, a lightweight knife with grippy pliers and a screwdriver end, a few zip ties for holding a backpack together, a tent pole splint, and several safety pins. Finally, your inflatable sleeping pad likely came with its own tiny repair kit, including an alcohol wipe and a matching repair patch with adhesive optimized for the pad material. This whole kit weighs three ounces and can help prevent some serious headaches.
