#8302. The Dean Fidelman Interview: 6 Photos, 6 Decades

A portrait of Dean Fidelman in 1971, the year he arrived in Yosemite. (Photo: Warren Shelton)

Dean Fidelman arrived in the Yosemite Valley in 1971 as a teenager. Yosemite has been his home ever since—except for a blip in the ‘80s, when he set aside his passion for climbing to become a fashion photographer in New York City and Los Angeles. But a phone call saved him from what was, for him, soulless commercial work.

It was Lynn Hill who called, asking Fidelman to start making climbing photos again. She invited him to come shoot her on some climbs in Europe, where he also first met Chris Sharma. From there, he doubled down on his life’s mission to show “the art of rock climbing,” in his words.

Fidelman spent the first half of his career shooting in black and white on film cameras, including a Pentax 6×7. He processed his own film and developed his own photos—sometimes by night in the historic Yosemite darkroom of Ansel Adams. Eventually, he caught up with the times when filmmaker Renan Ozturk gave him a Sony a7R II mirrorless camera and he made the switch to digital—and full color. “In my viewfinder, I set the preview to black and white, but the capture contains full color,” Fidelman told Climbing.

Now, 55 years after arriving in Yosemite, Fidelman still calls the area home and continues to shoot climbers around Camp 4. Perhaps best known for his work capturing the Yosemite Stonemasters and Stone Monkeys, Fidelman has also sat down for interviews in a couple documentaries released this year, including The Dark Wizard about Dean Potter, and a film about the weed plane that crashed in Yosemite, enriching many of his friends.

Fidelman is also known for his Stone Nudes, nude portraits of climbers bouldering or free soloing. He started the series in 1999 and now estimates it runs 300 images deep. At least a few times a year, he still receives requests from climbers to shoot a Stone Nude—a phrase which he has tattooed on his hands.

We caught up with Fidelman to discover the changes and throughlines he’s observed across six decades of Yosemite photography, the challenges of revisiting his relationship with Dean Potter for The Dark Wizard, and the next iteration of the Stone Nudes project. For this retrospective interview, we also asked Fidelman to select one photo for each decade of his work, which you’ll find below.

This interview has been edited for clarity and concision.

Dean Fidelman: As the decades have progressed, the way that I think about making a photograph has changed. But the people haven’t changed as much. With the Stonemasters, I was just making photographs of my friends doing cool things in the desert. I wasn’t really thinking about anything besides trying to make the best photograph I could—and finding out what a good photograph was.

With the Stone Monkeys, from the late ’90s until 2010 or 2015, I was simply living in Yosemite in the meadow, sleeping down by the river. So I fit in financially with this group of people really well. When I asked someone to make a photograph with me, there was no hesitation.

Recently, I’ve done some photographs for Summit Journal of people on YOSAR [Yosemite Search and Rescue] and at Camp 4. The first thing someone would say when I asked if I could make their photograph was, “I’d be honored.”

That kind of put me on the back foot in a weird way. If I ask to make a photograph of you, it’s because I respect you, or there’s something about you that I really enjoy being around or seeing. So it’s more like you’re honoring me, because you’re going to be vulnerable in front of my camera for a moment. Once we get over that, it’s just like working with the people I’ve always worked with.

Fidelman: When Lynn reconnected with me, it was pretty much immediate—”there it is.” You think of your path in a linear way that leads to being the best at something, but that’s not how it works. I was doing my photography much more personally than commercially. When Lynn connected with that, I thought, “Oh yeah, the personal aspect of photography, I can do that.” She definitely sponsored me and opened that world back up.

Fidelman: Charles Cole at Five Ten and John Bachar at Boreal both used me for ads. But Charles especially would say, “Here’s $500, here’s $1,000. Here’s my camera. Just give me some photos, but make what you’ve always made—no pressure.”

When I got back into Yosemite, one of the first people I met was Dean Potter. He was super open to me. I met him through Bachar because they were giving him shoes at the time and wanted to make some photographs. We had an immediate kinship, and that brought me deeper in with the Stone Monkeys. Then you had Cedar Wright, who was just starting off at that moment in time, and everyone else just came out of that.

With the people who survived—and the people who didn’t—I realized I was making this visual record of friends, trying to express them in the moment. That’s what I’ve hopefully continued to do.

Fidelman: Honestly, my opinion hasn’t changed since the ’70s. It wasn’t like I just happened by when Bachar or Yabo [John Yablonski] or somebody was doing a solo. Sometimes Bachar would say, “Hey, I’ve got this thing figured out now and I’m going to do it. I want you to make the photographs.” Three or four of us would jump in his van, go down to wherever the solo was, and make these photographs.

Even back then, climbing magazines did not want to publish [free soloing photos]. I didn’t take it personally. The first publication that published my work was the National Enquirer. It was a picture of Bachar soloing with a headline like “Man Climbs Rock” or “Daredevil Climbs Rock.”

So I experienced both ends of the spectrum early on. I realized that what you’re making isn’t going to be universally accepted. But you’re doing it for the people who are doing these solos and the people who appreciate it. I wasn’t making all this stuff happen; it was happening in front of me and has continued across generations.

Fidelman: When film crews called 10 years after Dean Potter died to make a film, I was really kind of conflicted, but I approached it as professionally as I could. They showed me a rough cut of all four episodes. After I watched, I went into this horrible depression that I just got out of in the last couple months.

Fidelman: It made him very real again. Suddenly, I still think he’s alive. He’s existing. I can feel his presence, trying to come up really close to me and intimidate me—his voice and everything. Obviously, it’s storytelling, but it’s made me really question a lot of what happened and a lot of who I was. I think hopefully I’ve gotten that straightened out.

Fidelman: It means having a high respect for unspoken boundaries—how you carry yourself in that moment, what your objective is, and what you can ask of the person in front of you. With Stone Nudes especially, they are naked and vulnerable. There’s all kinds of trust going on there. You respect unspoken boundaries by observing someone to see how open they are to direction. But I’ve also found women have been mansplained with men trying to tell them how to climb.

And then with your friends, you’re on an intimate level because they know you, but suddenly there’s a camera up. They’ve seen your work and they’re honored. So you need to try to get rid of that awkwardness by bringing your energy back and refocusing.

Fidelman: I’m still working on the Valley Muse book. I made some new Stone Nudes this March that I really like, so I’m looking at calendars or possibly a book, gathering for another five or six years, traveling to favorite spots and places I’ve always wanted to go to.

Fidelman: There are a couple of photographs I want to make in Patagonia. It’s just a boulder in the middle of nowhere—and there was so much nowhere. There’s also a cool volcanic place in Venezuela. But next, I’m heading to Spain to work on deep-water soloing nudes in Mallorca.

Fidelman: Probably 2018, right when I stopped with the Stone Nudes calendar and Renan [Ozturk] gave me that camera. That’s probably the last time I went into a darkroom, unless the darkroom had a scanner in it and I was scanning my negatives. With a lot of my original black and white photography, I would process the film myself. I used to find these traditional photo labs up and down the coast.

After the last lab closed, I used Ansel Adams’s darkroom in Yosemite. They would let me use the darkroom from 10 at night until midnight. What was left of it was just a long sink and a heavy dark curtain. I’d be rattling cans at midnight and I look over and there’s a portrait of Ansel looking at me like, “What are you doing in my darkroom?”

Fidelman: Once I was shooting in the middle of the Merced River by the 120/140 junction. A friend was on top of the boulder posing while I was waist-deep in the river. Suddenly, a big tour bus pulled over and a bus-load of tourists piled out, pushing each other trying to take photos with their phones.

One time I was making photographs in Eldorado Canyon on that boulder right in the middle of the river with my friend Anora, a hippie. I went back to Yosemite and processed the film in Ansel Adams’s darkroom. I’m hanging out at the lodge and this person comes up to me—obviously a climber, but very clean-cut. He goes, “Excuse me, are you Dean Fidelman?” And I go, “Yeah.”

He sticks his hand out, with this big smile on his face and goes, “I want to shake your hand. You were in Eldorado Canyon about a month ago and you were making some photos. We were on the Bastille and oh my God, she is so beautiful. That was the most amazing day. My partner went home and bought a calendar even though he knew she wasn’t going to be in that one. But is she going to be in the next one?”

Then I made a Stone Nude of my friend Brian Ludovici, who’s a wonderful human and a super cool boulderer. He asked if I would make a photograph of him on Midnight Lightning (V8) with his clothes on. So I show up there and he’s just got this pair of short shorts on, right? This is his favorite boulder problem. He loves it. He worships it. And he goes up it and down it. I say, “Hey, man. You think you could do it nude?” Maybe four or five of his friends are there, all egging him on. He gets to where he’s pressing out the mantle, but he couldn’t do it. He put his shorts back on.

Then there’s this guy running full blast toward me from 100 yards away. He looks really closely at Brian. Then he stops and goes, “Dude, this was the most amazing day of my life. I looked from over there by the kiosk and there was a beautiful nude woman doing Midnight Lightning, so I started running to get a closer look. But it’s a dude.”

Fidelman: One fall. My friend Joey was like, “Let’s make a photograph.” I first met her when she was 16. She goes, “I want to make a photograph.” I go, “No, no.” Same with [Chris] Sharma. I go, “No, you have to wait until you’re 18.”

A couple years later, she’s in Joshua Tree and wants to climb the White Rastafarian (V2). First, I tell her she has to do it with her clothes and shoes on, so I can see that she can do it. She does it perfectly. But she can’t do it barefoot. So, she took her clothes off and we had a bunch of pads down, hidden by the bushes. Three of her friends were spotting.

She gets up to the crux and starts to bring her hand up and she blows. Her friends didn’t even touch her. She hit the pads, but sprained her ankle fairly badly. I felt really horrible, but I did put it in [a calendar]. I always make certain that [climbers] can do it at least with their clothes on first. Now I always tell the spotters, “If you’ve got to get in the photo, don’t even worry about it. Put your hands on them, even though they’re naked!” Unless somebody wants to solo something, but it’s not going to be outside the limits—ever.

Fidelman: I’m working on two books. One is a history of the Nose with John Long, Hans Florine, Ed Hartouni, and Sarah Conley. The other is a book on the Stone Monkeys with James Lucas. We’re getting the manuscripts and photo selections organized, with plans to publish over the next couple of years.

Fidelman: I’ve been working on archiving all the stuff from the ‘60s and Glen [Denny] was a huge influence on me, as well as Tom Frost and and a few others.

I understood two things very early on. One is if you’ve tied into a rope with people who have climbed with people like John Salathé and Royal Robbins, you’ve tied into a rope with all those other people, too. I tied into a rope with [Jim] Bridwell and lots of people that probably go back all the way to Salathé.

When John Long and I made the Stonemaster book, it was a fulfillment of my dream to make a book, but also of the understanding that if we allow those stories to die, we have no magic. All our beliefs are based on those stories and those legends.

I’m hoping maybe someone shows up, and I don’t care who they are. If I can see that passion and they’re really looking to provide that rope that we can all tie into, then my work would move forward.

#8301. The 7 Items That Got Me Through October (and the Rest of Fall)

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Oh October, the month of mystery. Here in Boulder, Colorado, it’s when you wake up in the dark not knowing if it will be warm, cold, raining, or windy. The only thing you do know every morning is there will be even more much-larger-than-life-sized skeletons poking out of peoples’ lawns. (Why has this become a thing? As my friend Clare said on a run the other day, “people are desecrating their lawns with plastic trash!”)

Anyway, it’s a tricky time of year for running. Head out the door overdressed and you will end up a puddle of sweat that, depending on the weather, ultimately makes you cold. Leave underdressed, as I did for a tempo run two weeks ago, and your limbs will feel like they’ve been cursed by a witch who’s turned them to immovable ice.

But tricky conditions can be solved with treats. My trusty associate editor is, in his words, “going to the desert to do something stupid.” (Go Cade!) That leaves just me to round up our gear of the month. Here are the five items I kept packed in my Janji Ultrahauler (another piece of gear I can’t live without!) so I was ready for whatever I woke up to:

Kilian Jornet’s fledgling shoe and apparel company has stuck to relatively technical alpine equipment—until now with the Nnormal Cadi. This do-everything trail shoe is exceptionally comfortable thanks to a padded heel collar and tongue and a cushy midsole with 37 mm stack in the heel, 31 mm in the forefoot. It’s got a nice wide toe box (an obsession of mine as I work on my foot strength and toe splay). And with a Vibram Megagrip outsole it’s tacky on all terrain and in all conditions. I also appreciate the mesh upper, which is breathable on hot days and dries quickly on wet ones. It’s the only shoe I brought on a trip recently, which means I found myself wearing it for a 12-mile run around the Charles River in Boston—definitely not as energetic as your typical road trainer these days, but it got the job done just fine. It’s just a solid, dependable shoe.

It’s rained A LOT in Boulder this month. And by a lot, I mean more than zero times. I know I’ve lived here for too long because I’ve gotten soft and the only thing that got me through more than zero very dark, very wet mornings was this rain jacket from Arc’teryx. That’s because it’s actually waterproof. But it’s also super lightweight and breathable, meaning you don’t incinerate in your own body heat and end up wet anyway. Plus one for the cinch on the hood so you can actually keep it on your head while you’re running and another bonus for the vents under the armpits, which help moderate body heat. I know $450 is an obscene amount to spend on anything, but this is definitely a case of you get what you pay for.

When it comes to running pants and tights I am very, very picky. They can’t suffocate my waist, but they also need to stay put. They can’t bunch around the knees, but they also can’t be so baggy that the pant legs rub into each other. The Janji Altas Multi Pant is one of the few pieces that passes my stringent test. They are supremely comfortable thanks to a wide elastic waistband, and a drawstring lets you dial in the fit. They’re loose enough to allow for full range of motion, but they’re streamlined enough that I can wear them for harder efforts without getting annoyed. Why I really love them for this time of year is they are lightweight and breathable, providing just the right amount of insulation. And even better, they have nearly knee-length ankle zips so I often wear them for the warm up and zip them off for intervals—no shoe removal required.

There is something so comforting and luxurious about tucking into a comfy vest for a fall outing. Enter this fleece-lined vest from 7Mesh. It’s super breathable yet cozy thanks to a soft, woven outer layer paired with the light and ultrasoft fleece lining. I’ve been loving it for colder runs when a jacket feels like too much but a long sleeve isn’t quite enough. And I’ve also been loving it on the bike—especially because the vest folds into itself via a big back pocket, revealing little straps that let you fix it to your bike frame when you’re not wearing it.

Not too cold and not too warm, snug but not tight, these gloves are  a shoulder-season star. They’re so lightweight that I don’t think twice about wearing them for the start of a run before the sun rises and stashing them in a pocket as I warm up with the ground. I can use my phone with them on, carry my ballot (the midterms are on Tuesday!), as well as maneuver zippers and, if desperate, tie shoes. Plus the colors and patterns instantly boost my mood. (They came in so many fun options!)

One-star review for the name. Zero stars for the logo branded on the top of the collar. And yet, five stars for these socks. They are just that comfy and moisture-wicking. I am pretty skeptical of overengineered gear, but CEP has me thinking maybe there is something to developing stuff in a lab. These socks provide a gentle amount of compression and arch support while also being ventilated in all the places you want it. In other words: they stay put, and they keep my feet comfortable for a wide range of temperatures—perfect for fall running. Most importantly, my feet do not slip in my shoes. I repeat: no slippage here. My friend saw me running in them the other day and he said he also loves these socks so much that he ordered five pairs. Oh and they come in approximately one billion colorways.

I know, I know, it’s a crime to spend more than $50 on a hair product—much less two products. But hear me out: Colorado is savage on my wavy hair. When left unchecked, the dry air and harsh sun leech out every last drop of moisture, turning my hair into a wiry mess. Add in the rainy days of October (or my annual pilgrimage to Hawaii) and in years past I am ripping out chunks of matted hair every time I shower. Enter this fancy shampoo and conditioner. I am not exaggerating when I say this stuff has revolutionized my hair’s life. For the first time in 13 years since I moved here, my hair feels soft. And I can actually get a brush through it when I get out of the shower! You better believe I will be buying it again.

#8300. 31,000 Miles, 28 Years: Karl Bushby’s Walk Around the World by the Numbers

Karl Bushby walks through a park in Peterborough, England, on October 22, 2026, during the final leg of his 28-year Goliath Expedition. (Photo: Leon Neal/Getty Images)

On November 1, 1998, Karl Bushby left Punta Arenas, Chile, and began walking north. Ahead of him, the 29-year-old British former paratrooper pushed a modified golf trolley filled with supplies and gear that he dubbed “The Beast.” His goal: to walk as far as a person could in unbroken footsteps on Earth, without using anything but his own hands and feet to make forward progress. His planned route for what he called the Goliath Expedition would take him from the southernmost tip of South America to his hometown of Hull, England, a journey he estimated would take him about 12 years.

Exactly 28 years and one day later, Bushby arrived back in Hull’s Queen Victoria Square to cheering crowds at shortly before noon on November 2, capping off a journey that was much longer—and far more complicated—than he could have imagined when he began. Along the way, he navigated shifting ice floes across the Bering Strait and swam the Caspian Sea to dodge geopolitical tensions and the English Channel after Eurotunnel refused to let him walk through the service tunnels connecting France and the UK. Not all the obstacles were physical, either: Bushby decamped to Mexico to regroup after his sponsorships dried up in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis and spent 10 years crossing Russia, stymied by visa requirements and an entry ban. (He finally received the permission he needed in 2014 after walking 3,600 miles across the United States to Russia’s embassy.)

All of that added up to something larger than a hike—a journey that ended up taking almost exactly half of the 57-year-old’s life. (It demanded a commensurate sacrifice, and not just from him. Bushby has a son, now 36, who he’s only seen a handful of times since leaving, and a 12-year-old granddaughter he had never met until finishing his trek; he also had and lost two long-term romantic relationships during the journey.)

For all that, the man behind the Goliath Expedition isn’t inclined to brag. When Backpacker writer Bill Donahue caught up with Bushby in Mexico in 2012, at what would turn out to be the halfway point of his walk, Bushby downplayed his own achievements.

“I’m an average guy,” Bushby said. “I’m less than average. I’m an underachiever. All I’m doing is putting one foot in front of the other.”

Here’s what Bushby’s big walk looked like by the numbers.

The approximate distance that Bushby walked from Punta Arenas, Chile, to Hull, England. That’s equivalent to 14 thru-hikes of the Appalachian Trail, 1.25 times the circumference of the globe, or roughly 13 percent of the average distance from the Earth to the Moon. That distance took him through 30 countries, according to the Associated Press.

The total distance Bushby had to swim during his trip. That included roughly 179 miles across the Caspian Sea in September and October 2024 and 21 miles across the English Channel in October 2026. Bushby did both of those swims in stages, resting on a support boat at night and returning to the coordinates where he had gotten out of the water in the morning.

The amount of time Bushby spent in jail after crossing borders without authorization. That includes 18 days in Panamanian custody after he crossed the roadless Darién Gap from Colombia and 58 days in Russian detention following his crossing of the Bering Strait from Alaska.

Bushby’s average pace across his entire trip. While far slower than other long-distance hikers—the small group of people to have hiked 10,000 miles in a year all had to knock off roughly 28 miles per day—the legal and financial hurdles Bushby faced, as well as his refusal to use transportation to bypass complicated terrain, meant that making miles was significantly more difficult for him.

The number of carts that Bushby used to carry his gear during the Goliath Expedition. The first, the Beast, survived three years before breaking down in Nicaragua. He used its replacement, the Beast 2, for the remaining 25 years. In an interview with The Guardian, Bushby called the cart “my Wilson,” referring to Tom Hanks’ famous volleyball and conversation partner from Castaway.

#8299. The Best Midlayers for Men and Women (2027)

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

November 2026: After testing 63 midlayers while hiking, skiing, fat-biking and climbing in wintry weather, we named the Arc’teryx Atom Hoody our Best Overall pick for its do-it-all balance of warmth, breathability, and weather protection. The most durable option is Mountain Hardwear’s Kor Alloy Jacket. The best for ultra-cold conditions is the Marmot WarmCube Active Novus Hoody.

Midlayers have an outrageously demanding job description. Unlike the super-puffy parkas and belay jackets that we wear to stay warm while hunkering down, midlayers provide insulation during activity—a role that calls for a true multi-tasker. Its duties include keeping us warm while venting excess heat, whisking away sweat, and shielding us from the elements. It’s a tall order, yet our testing team found six insulated midlayer jackets that check all the boxes.

These breathable insulators successfully regulated testers’ temperatures while they skied, hiked, biked, and ran in winter weather conditions. Testers typically sandwiched these jackets between a base layer and a waterproof shell. On climbs, or in dry weather when they ditched the shell, testers also evaluated these toppers for their ability to shed precipitation and buffer gusts.

Sizes: XS-XXXL (men’s), XXS-XXL (women’s) Weight: 12.5 oz. (men’s), 11.3 oz. (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Balanced performance + Extended sizes + Lots of pockets – Lacks abrasion resistance

The Atom has been one of our favorite midlayers since its debut in 2009, and its design has hardly changed over the years except for sustainability upgrades. With stretchy fleece side and underarm panels bridging generous helpings of synthetic insulation in the torso, hood, and arms, it strikes the ideal balance of warmth and breathability for cold weather conditions. We found the Atom’s insulated panels—packed with 60 grams of polyester loft—plenty warm down to the teens without an outer layer while skinning and bootpacking in the Tetons. One tester, who wore his hoody ice climbing in Silverton, Colorado, called the Atom’s mix of insulation and breathable fleece “perfectly balanced.”

The unconfining cut fits most bodies, small or large, and two hand pockets and one internal chest pocket secure valuables. The cinchable hood is big enough for a helmet, which came in handy when temps plummeted during one Idaho-based tester’s fat-bike ride in the Tetons. The fabric’s fluorocarbon-free DWR finish repelled drizzle during late-November training runs. But the Atom delivers too much insulation for mild conditions and shoulder seasons (at 35 degrees and above, consider the Atom SL.) And although the breathable fabric feels soft next to skin, it gets pilly after repeated encounters with pack straps and other abrasive tools.

Sizes: S-XL (men’s), XS-XL (women’s) Weight: 18 oz. (men’s), 15.6 oz. (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Attractive patterning + Warm – Large packed size

Proving that midlayers don’t have to be thick and bulky to provide significant warmth, this Merino-stuffed puffy goes relatively light on the filling (80-percent wool with biodegradable, bio-based polyester). But even on a 5-degree day in the Tetons, one tester comfortably wore this midlayer while yo-yo-ing backcountry slopes. That wool/synthetic blend stays warm when wet and doesn’t accumulate body odor after a season of sweat. It also scores high marks for sustainability: Ortovox sources wool from sheep living in the German Alps for a shorter supply chain, and the jacket’s shell and lining fabrics use 100-percent recycled polyamide.

Veering from the sausage-casing cut of most Ortovox apparel, this boxy jacket easily accommodates underlayers and pairs best with a loose, freeride-style shell. The matte shell fabric proved plenty abrasion-resistant when worn beneath a pack, and the fabric ably buffered gusts. Testers also liked it at the resort, when the airy fit and naturally regulating insulation (wool breathes better than synthetic fills) kept them comfortable through hard efforts and chilling lift rides. But the teeny zipper pull is tricky to operate with or without gloves, and packability isn’t great, owing to the jacket’s generous cut and less-compressible wool fill.

Sizes: S-XXL (men’s), XS-XL (women’s) Weight: 11 oz. (men’s), 9.5 oz. (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Abrasion-resistant + Warm for the weight – Expensive

Here’s an armor-tough jacket that actually breathes—an uncommon combination that made it our Idaho tester’s new go-to. “I’m tired of tearing and patching midlayers,” he said. But this nylon ripstop is far more abrasion- and tear-resistant than anything else I’ve used.” That outer shell uses two versions of 20-denier Pertex Quantum Air: A coated variety on the front body and sleeves to repel precip, and an uncoated stretchy one for the underarms and back. Inside, a ventilating lining made of polyester Octa fibers (called AirMesh) and 40-gram PrimaLoft Gold Active insulation (60-percent recycled) deliver breathable warmth.

The combination creates a highly versatile layer. “From resort skiing at Bogus Basin, wearing it under my shell, to skinning the backcountry at Mores Creek Summit, to climbing at Leslie Gulch and The Fins, this midlayer kept me comfortable, and it didn’t tear while bushwacking or being brushed against rocks,” reported one tester.

Four front pockets hold a satellite communicator and other essentials, and are placed out of the way for belaying and active climbing. Fit is just right—accommodating underlayers without bagging—and the lack of a hood trims unnecessary bulk. But it’s not as warm as some other jackets in test; we found it best used in temperatures above 20 degrees.

When effort and conditions change, this is the breathable, ultralight midlayer that will keep you free and regulated all day long. The PrimaLoft Active Evolve fleece manages your temperature and keeps you dry without trapping heat. The stretch knit has an athletic fit that doesn’t restrict mobility, so you can scramble, climb, and transition on the pitch with ease and comfort. It’s also compact, stowing away into a hidden neck pocket with an elastic cinch and carry tab, so you can stash it away whenever you need to drop a layer.

Sizes: S-XXXL (men’s), XS-XXL (women’s) Weight: 12 oz. (men’s), 10.4 oz. (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Sweat-wicking + Very compressible – Minimal insulation

The Dawner is basically a stretchy windbreaker with a fleece liner, making it an all-season midlayer for high-energy activities like cross-country skiing, running, summit-bagging, fat-biking, and more; this was one of our testers’ most-worn pieces thanks to its versatility.

The supple, 20-denier stretch nylon shell (with nine percent Spandex) has a DWR finish that sheds light rain (but won’t hold up in a storm), while 100-gram Octaknit insulation—one of the lightest, most breathable polyester fleeces on the market—lines the interior. It’s exactly what testers wanted while moving fast: the fuzzy interior mopped up sweat as quickly as they produced it, and the lightweight insulation complemented high-output body heat.

The jacket’s generous cut fits over thicker baselayers, yet it’s slick enough to slip under heavier shells. A cinchable helmet-compatible hood and hem made it easy to batten down the hatches during cold starts on pre-dawn backcountry missions. And because it packs down to the size of a grapefruit, it migrated into our Teton tester’s pack for summertime mountaineering adventures too. But this is no super-toaster: During light exertion or in cold temps below 15 degrees, testers wanted something warmer.

Sizes: S-XL (men’s), XS-XL (women’s) Weight: 13 oz. (men’s), 11 oz. (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Excellent breathability + Stretchy and unconfining – Not for large bodies

When breathability bests warmth in the Roshambo contest between jackets, this hybrid insulator wins. The First Light 1.0 Stretch Hoody is zoned for high-output activity, with most of its insulation (thin panels of PrimaLoft Gold Active) in the chest, hood and outer arms. The back and underarms are made of a Merino wool jersey (knit with 46 percent nylon) that’s supremely stretchy and breathable. The 20-denier stretch-nylon shell fabric has a DWR finish to repel light snow.

“It works perfectly with a pack—my back is where I usually get too hot and sweaty,” said our Tahoe area tester, who wore it for a season of cross-country skiing, touring, and resort snowboarding (when he topped it with a shell). Testers felt that this jacket worked best in cool to cold temps above 20 degrees.

Packability earned praise, with the whole jacket tucking into the zippered chest pocket around the size of a liter bottle. Two zippered hand pockets and a helmet-sized hood round out the features. The hood lacks adjustability, but our ski-touring tester deemed it functional during above-treeline deployment. Downsides? Sizing tops out at XL, and the jacket fits snug, even on slim builds.

Sizes: S-XXL (men’s), XS-XL (women’s) Weight: 17 oz. (men’s), 15 oz. (women’s)

Pros and Cons + Highly insulating + Doesn’t feel bulky – Not weather resistant

This jacket’s triumph is the way it pairs heavyweight insulation—testers wore it in temperatures from 10 below zero to 15 degrees—with outstanding breathability and mobility.

That’s achieved by surrounding plump squares of “featherless” synthetic insulation (polyester flakes that imitate the soft, body-conforming feel of down) with uninsulated strips that promote mobility and ventilation. “It let me move around a lot in cold weather without overheating,” reports our New Hampshire tester after wearing it while backcountry skiing near Zealand Falls Hut and hiking around Franconia Notch. “The gaps in the baffling allow for so much airflow, yet that maximized airflow somehow doesn’t compromise heat retention,” she explains.

Those air channels are just as good at letting wind in, however, so our testers topped this jacket with a shell whenever conditions grew gusty or wet (the 100-percent preconsumer recycled nylon ripstop doesn’t offer much protection beyond drizzle). “This jacket is surprisingly sleek for a puffy, so it doesn’t feel bulky when I wear it under a shell,” said one tester who stayed cozy in it while skiing Sugarloaf in 10-degree temperatures.

Two zippered hand pockets and two internal drop pouches secure handwarmers or a collapsible flask (our fat-biking tester loved this storage for keeping water from freezing). The fit, however, is universally roomy: Some shoppers may want to size down.

Selecting a midlayer is all about finding the sweet spot for your activity and weather conditions. Unlike heavy down hoodies and parkas meant for sitting around camp or belaying ice climbers, midlayers need to keep you warm while also offering breathability.

The warmth-to-breathability ratio is key: In general, a great midlayer should keep you warm, but not so warm that you overheat and soak it with sweat. Protection from wind and precipitation is a bonus, but midlayers are often paired with a waterproof shell in bad weather, so finding that magic warmth-breathability balance should be your priority.

Synthetic fabric and insulation are key to almost all midlayers. Fleece-backed jackets, with their porous fibers, offer the best breathability, but can often be too thin and permeable for very cold or windy conditions. Hybrid or “body-mapped” designs that blend baffled panels with other fabrics are excellent when working up a sweat in colder conditions. Minimally vented synthetic insulated jackets provide the most warmth at the cost of breathability, although they are still a better choice than sweating it out in a down puffy.

Here’s how to decide which midlayer is right for you:

If you are planning to work up a lather, look for breathable layers that will keep you from getting clammy, which can make you hypothermic if you stop moving or encounter big winds. Fleece-backed jackets, like the Stio Dawner (which uses loosely knit Octa fibers), are king when it comes to breathability. If conditions are too windy or frigid, however, ramping up to a midlayer with some synthetic fill, like the Arc’teryx Atom, is a better choice.

Down-filled layers have the best warmth-to-weight ratio when it comes to outdoor gear, but quickly lose that advantage if you’re sweating from the inside or getting soaked from the outside. Synthetic fill (used in most midlayers reviewed here) and fleece-backed jackets keep you warm when wet. So does wool (the Ortovox Ravine Metawool 90), though it does absorb water over time and becomes a soggier, heavier insulator.

If you know it’s going to be frigid or you’ll be moving slow, by all means, go for a thicker puffy like the Marmot WarmCube Active Novus. But if you’re moving fast in typical winter temps, chances are that much insulation will be overkill. It’s not a bad idea to pack two midlayers, or at least include a fleece in your kit, to be prepared for changing temperatures and exertion levels.

If you plan to wear a wind- and waterproof shell over your midlayer, you won’t need to worry about the storm cutting right down to your base layers. If not, look for a piece that offers some wind and water resistance, like the Ortovox Ravine Metawool 90 or Arc’teryx Atom.

Q: What’s the best type of insulation for midlayers?

A: Moisture-resistant synthetic or wool insulation does the best job at maintaining warmth when exposed to sweat and light precipitation. Synthetics come in a range of fibers and constructions, including carpet-like fleeces, sheets of batting, and loose fibers that get sewn into baffles to imitate the warmth and appearance of down (but with superior moisture resistance).

Q: Should I get a midlayer with a hood or without?

A: Depends on how many other hooded jackets you’ll layer with it. A hooded midlayer provides additional warmth and weather protection, but heavy snow can soak it unless you cover it with a shell—which can add up to surplus headwear. A hoodless midlayer under a hooded shell is generally a better choice for stormy conditions.

Q: Why are there no down puffies among the midlayers in this review?

A: Down loses its insulating qualities when it gets damp (as it will when worn as a midlayer for sweaty pursuits). Looking for a technical down jacket? Read on.

Q: Why are midlayer jackets so expensive?

A: Making materials that are simultaneously warm, breathable, and protective is a technological feat that doesn’t come cheap. These multi-tasking materials cost more than ones that do just one job well.

Our testers spend a lot of time outdoors—they qualify as obsessive skiers, mountaineers, ultrarunners, climbers, hikers, and view-admirers. But they also possess the gift of gab. Our testers must be able to say much more about a piece of gear than “it’s awesome” or “it sucks.” They sweat details about, well, sweat, and how apparel responds to their sweat or contributes to its production. They note what makes a jacket feel unconfining, how much wind protection it delivers, and whether it plays nice with a backpack.

For this test, we evaluated 46 of the most breathable midlayers on the market, including full-zip and pullover styles. We asked testers to consider the fit, the breathability, the warmth they enjoyed from each midlayer, and its best application: Is the jacket best for ski-race spectating? Nordic skiing? Après at the resort? All of the above? Only the items that earned raves on performance and livability won coverage among these reviews.

Kelly Bastone moved to the Colorado Rockies in 1998 and has pursued outdoor sports ever since. A freelancer who writes about gear and other outdoor topics for publications such as Backpacker, AFAR, and The Red Bulletin, Bastone has contributed many gear reviews to Outside over the years. An avid skier (resort, Nordic and backcountry), fly-fisher, mountain biker and mushroom forager, she gets the news she needs from the weather report.

#8298. How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

Joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September. He guessed he’d be maybe 20 or 30 minutes behind in the early miles.

But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.

“That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner. “But I told myself that maybe he went out at more of a race effort, while my pace was better for a multi-day FKT.”

McConaughy, known by his thru-hiking trail name, “Stringbean,” has more than a few multiday FKTs to his name. He’s set records on the Pacific Crest Trail, Appalachian Trail, Long Trail, and Arizona Trail. And he had two prior record attempts on the JMT, one of which earned him an unsupported FKT.

“I thought my experience could help me beat him,” McConaughy said.

As he chased the ghost of the JMT’s past, McConaughy drew from his many multi-day FKTs and races. All of the miles and mistakes, successes and failures, and lessons and growth along the way helped him ultimately establish a new FKT of 2 days, 16 hours, and 15 seconds, taking nearly three and a half hours off a time that had stood for nearly a decade.

In rock climbing, climbers talk about “flashing” a route. It’s when they successfully climb the whole thing on their first attempt—without any practice or “beta” to help. McConaughy’s JMT effort was pretty much the opposite of flashing. The 33-year-old Seattle-based endurance coach was incredibly familiar with every mile of the JMT. Prior to his record setting attempt this fall, he’d covered the trail four times—the first in 2014—including the two prior FKT attempts. He’d also spent five summers guiding backpacking trips in the Sierra.

So when McConaughy ended up in a blizzard on Muir Pass with snowflakes landing in his eyeballs, it didn’t really stress him out or slow him down. If anything, it helped him move faster as he wanted to get up and over to warmer ground.

“I’ve seen the worst that the Sierra can throw at you,” he said, citing thunderstorms, blizzards, and rugged terrain. “I didn’t have to do a bunch of mental gymnastics, worrying about things I hadn’t experienced before. Instead, I could devote all of my energy to things that actually were issues.”

Most of McConaughy’s issues during the record attempt were ones he expected to occur, was prepared for, and could handle. “The long climbs were long climbs and some of the descents take decades,” he said. But after numerous JMT attempts he knew “it could feel much harder.” A little over a day into his attempt he was two hours ahead of D’Haene’s splits.

The JMT is far from the only goal for which McConaughy’s persistence has paid off. He took seven swings at earning a Golden Ticket into the Western States 100 before clinching one at the Black Canyon 100K on his eighth try in 2025. He’s also raced the Cocodona 250 three times and has a trio of Barkley Marathons starts.

“I like to think I’m more fun than a project-er, but when I look back, that’s pretty much my entire running career,” he said. “I feel like it gives me purpose. I want to do routes that inspire me and motivate me and take what I’ve done wrong, or what I feel like I could improve on, and continue to experiment, tinker, and optimize.”

He’s not as intense as a rock climber going after a seemingly impossible objective like the Dawn Wall, he swears. Rather, it’s about finding the sweet spot where he’s pushing himself to grow but having fun doing it. He’s not training to be the best at any given race or record attempt; he’s training to be the best version of himself for years to come.

“I get a lot of joy from sticking with the process, training with a smile, putting in the work to make a difference, and looking for opportunities to rise like a phoenix and perform the best that I can,”  McConaughy said.

Caroline Himbert, who is coached by McConaughy and set her own unsupported FKT on the JMT this July, helped pace McConaughy on the JMT this fall. “He goes back to things he’s failed at and tries to continuously learn and grow; he loves the science and spreadsheets and takes things seriously,” Himbert said. “But at the same time, he doesn’t take things too seriously and he keeps things fluid and fun.”

As evidenced by the fact that it stood for nine years, the JMT record was stout. D’Haene is known for bringing a newfound level of professionalism to FKT attempts, with a full support staff, set of pacers, and film crew. But rather than seeing the competitive level of the record as a deterrent, McConaughy saw it as part of the draw.

“It’s the granddaddy of FKTs,” he said. “More people have attempted the JMT FKT than pretty much any other premier route that exists—and the fact that François [D’Haene] and Darcy [Piceu] were the [previous] record holders is an ode to the level of attention and competitiveness that it’s gotten.”

On his first attempt in 2022, McConaughy set an unsupported record of three days and one hour. But Jeff Garmire beat it by 13 minutes just 25 days later.

McConaughy knew he could do better, so he tried to reclaim the record in 2024. But he hallucinated in the final miles and wound up off-trail on a class-four scramble, much closer to life-and-limb-threatening risk than he’d anticipated. It was a wake-up call for McConaughy, who always considers what he’s asking of others when he chases a big goal. He’s now the father of a 6-month-old and knew he couldn’t end up in a similar situation—or worse—if he went back.

“That experience made me really rethink what the record meant to me and ask myself if I wanted to do it again,” he said, adding that it felt reckless to go for another unsupported record. But after much reflection, and many conversations with his wife Katie, he decided he had to go back.

“I knew I couldn’t exist as an athlete without trying to put my stamp on the JMT,” he said. “This was my third time [attempting the FKT] on this trail and I wanted to give it my all, and use my best tips and tricks from every other effort to get the record.”

McConaughy showed up with a 12-tab spreadsheet and 12 years of beta to guide his effort this fall. He thought some of the greatest opportunities for improvement lay in fueling, pacing, and recruiting an all-star crew to help him out. In his unsupported-style attempts, he’d had to carry all of his own food and gear with no supply restocks along the way.

At Cocodona in 2025, McConaughy hit a wall that no amount of carbs could fix. He thought he knew how he needed to fuel to compete for the win. He’d done sweat testing and was experimenting with high-carb fueling. But he ended up with GI distress and struggled to breathe. He still finished in a respectable fourth place, but it was far from the finish he wanted.

He started working with nutritionist Meredith Terranova, who suggested he was likely hypernatremic—too high of blood sodium concentration—during Cocodona. He wondered if trying to optimize his performance through a data-driven approach with high carb fueling and sweat tests meant he’d stopped listening to his body.

So on the JMT he turned to real food like trail mix, purees, and waffles, especially on the big climbs—of which there is no shortage with 38,000 feet of elevation gain to cover. He also used recovery drink mixes and fat- and protein-based fuels from his nutrition sponsor, Näak.

“I feel like sticking to more whole food was the biggest learning and the biggest difference maker in my performance,” he said.

He also made up ground through a smarter sleep strategy. In his 2022 attempt, in which he finished six hours behind D’Haene’s record time, McConaughy slept for six hours. He knew there was an opportunity to trim down time spent resting while still sleeping enough to avoid dangerous hallucinations.

He settled on taking a mere 40 minutes of sleep beneath a pine tree on Bear Ridge—around 28 hours in. He thought it might be prudent to get at least an hour but he decided to push it a little with 40 minutes, figuring he could always nap later if he needed it. When he got to his third night out on the trail he was still running strong, cracking jokes, and appreciating his surroundings, Himbert said.

“You could tell he was having a good time and he was a ball of energy,” she said. “I was with him more towards the end, and he was still moving so well. I think that’s the key with this trail; it’s so challenging but if you can still move well towards the end then you can crack these times. I think Joe really nailed it, and it went close to perfect.”

McConaughy’s crew was one of his greatest assets. He learned some things about crewing the JMT after his crew missed him at Kearsarge Pass during his Pacific Crest Trail FKT in 2014. The PCT overlaps with the JMT for about 170 miles. He had to keep going on the PCT for two days with no sleeping bag, only a half-day’s worth of calories, and nothing warmer than a thin windbreaker. “We didn’t really know what we were doing,” he said. Hence the 12-tab spreadsheet this go-around, which was largely for the benefit of his crew and the complicated logistics of supporting a record-attempt on the JMT.

Part of the beauty of the JMT is that it offers an uninterrupted tour of backcountry wilderness. The trail only crosses the road twice over the course of the entire 223 miles. That’s also what makes it a bear to support. Meeting McConaughy on the trail required hiking several miles and thousands of feet of climbing to deliver food and gear. Pacers ran monster sections—usually around 40 miles at a time. But his crew of pacers was up for the challenge, with a collective résumé that boasted JMT FKTs, podium finishes, and 200-mile runs.

“Tara Dower talked about being a vessel on the Appalachian Trail, and I certainly had a similar experience on the JMT,” McConaughy said. “I was able to appreciate the beauty of where I was and the excitement of doing this absurd endurance thing because my crew was always filling my cup instead of making me pour things out to keep going.”

One thing that McConaughy has learned time and time again, is that he runs best when his cup is full.

“Gratitude and joy are the greatest performance-enhancing drugs,” he said.

While he was running, he thought about Katie, who was home solo-parenting so he could acclimatize to the altitude and run for 64 straight hours. He thought about his parents, who enabled him to get outside and run cross-country from a young age. He thought about the people who have supported his running career, and the friends who traveled to the Sierra to help him through the 223-mile journey. And he thought about the Sierra themselves, the mountains that have kept him coming back time and time again for the last 12 years.

“I run my worst when I’m thinking about how far behind someone’s splits I am,” he said. “When I caught myself doing that on the JMT, I thought, ‘This is doing more harm than good. You need to move forward at your own pace, and focus on the things that really matter.’”

After shaving over three hours off such a long-standing record, McConaughy hopes that he’s reached an end with his JMT FKT attempts. With all of the time and effort he has dedicated to the JMT, it feels a bit like a fairytale ending: “The princess was saved,” he said.

Now, he’s ready for a new goal, one he’s ready to chase to fuel his performance and fill his cup

“It’s one of those moments where I realize I’m maybe more capable than I thought I was,” he said. “And that makes it exciting to go back to Cocodona, or Western States, or another FKT, or any number of things to see what I can do.”

#8297. Meet the French Soldiers Who Get Paid to Climb Hard Alpine Routes

Dream jobs come in all shapes and sizes. Some might consider my job at Climbing dreamy. Others might hope to hangboard their way into professional climbing one day. My former colleague Duane Raleigh once made a very serious list of climber “dream jobs” that included roofers, fast food cooks, and snow shovelers.

I am here to tell you that none of these jobs are the best climber jobs. The actual best job for a climber, without any shadow of a doubt, is to be a member of the French military’s 27th Mountain Infantry Brigade. Why?

Allow me to describe the group’s latest work trip.

Last Wednesday, October 14, Sergeant Konrad Piontek and Corporals Amaury Fouillade and Clovis Paulin stood on the 6,654-meter summit of Peak 41 in Nepal. On the 1,400-meter North Face, they had just opened a stunning new route linking long sections of vertical ice with burly rock roofs and pitches of deep snow. They called the line Bon Matin (ED+ WI5+ M6 A1 90° snow), which translates to “Good Morning.” (Not sure what “ED+” means? Check out this article about international alpine grades.)

The three first ascensionists were part of a team of six from the 27th Mountain Infantry Brigade, better known as the Groupe Militaire de Haute Montagne, or GMHM. They had arrived in Nepal in mid-September along with a military doctor. After a period of acclimatization, the group split into two rope teams according to their skill level and how well each had adjusted to the altitude.

The Piontek-Fouillade-Paulin team eyed an attractive, unclimbed smear running plumb down Peak 41’s north side, to the left of a Korean team’s route from 2016. They began climbing on October 11 and summited after “four days of particularly committed climbing,” according to a statement shared with Climbing.

Over the 1,400 meters of the face, the team had to deal with numerous steep and poorly protected pitches, including sections of vertical snow. “We weren’t expecting pitches as steep as that, especially in snow,” said Corporal Paulin in the statement. But they also climbed what can only be described as truly classic mixed terrain: solid rock and squeaky ice, hanging above tons of exposure.

After summiting, the team descended the peak’s southeastern aspect via 15 rappels and significant downclimbing, turning their outing into one massive loop back to basecamp. “Reaching the summit was a real physical relief,” said Corporal Fouillade. “The mental release came later.”

Officially, France’s 10-person GMHM is tasked with “mastering extreme terrestrial environments, particularly vertical terrain and high altitude,” said a spokesperson to Climbing. This fluency in alpine terrain aims to contribute to the development of the entire French army’s mountain capabilities.

“The whole point of the GMHM is to practice high level alpinism,” said the group’s spokesperson. “What is learned regarding mountaineering or cold weather environments is passed on to the French mountain units, but the GMHM has otherwise no militaristic purposes.”

Similar mountain-military units exist across the globe, but—tragically—nothing so geared toward climbing excellence exists in North America. (If you happen to have a French passport and the pre-requisites, I’d be refreshing this recruitment page regularly.)

As far as we know, there is no fixed contract length for GMHM members; some alpinists have been part of the dream team for years and years.

In addition to one high-altitude expedition each year, the group travels to Greenland to teach the Groupement de Commandos de Montagne (literally: “mountain commandos”) about how to thrive in cold weather. They also take minor trips to develop rock and ice climbing skills, whether that’s locally in the French Alps or abroad to Yosemite. In plain terms, that means that 10 climbers get to occasionally don camo and earn a decent government salary to climb full time, around the world.

Did I mention the GMHM is the ultimate dream job?

#8296. Does Anti-Stink Clothing Actually Work? We (Really) Wanted to Find Out

It wasn't easy, and didn't go as expected, but the no stink clothes seemed to work as advertised. (Photo: Sam Anderson)

I boarded a 3-hour flight wearing a T-shirt I’d worn for over three weeks straight.

By this point I only had a vague sense of what I smelled like. Sleeping bag sweat? Iso gas? Hot dog water? I listened to the crew make the “very full flight” announcement again and shifted in my middle seat. It wasn’t just that I had a dirty shirt on—I’d barely showered for the entire trip, and apart from a few bracing dips in rivers and ocean water, I had made little effort to clean myself at all.

Instead, techy fabrics from Patagonia and an innovative startup called HercLéon battled my oils and odors at point-blank.

Except for deodorant, all that guarded the packed flight from trail stank were various items of “laundry-free” or “anti-odor” clothing. My Patagonia pants and sun hoodie were treated with steam-extracted, food-grade mint oil. The HercLéon T-shirt and my boxer briefs were infused with charcoal and woven with copper fibers. I had used exfoliating nylon washcloths from Lunatec that “never need washing.”

When I planned to hike through the majority of Washington state on a former rail grade, I immediately thought it would be helpful to bring only one set of clothes. But if I tried it and anything went wrong, I could be exposed. As is the case on many long-distance hikes, I knew clothes shopping could be a tough ask depending on where I was.

Still, wardrobe weight is real, and weight quickly becomes the enemy of comfort. So could materials like Patagonia’s HeiQ and HercLeon’s HercCopper limit foul smells after days on trail? Could that improve my overall mood, along with the weight savings, and could it all help me with social graces along the way?

My target was a 330-mile segment of the Great American Rail Trail. It links old railroad corridors from the western Cascades to the Idaho border, dividing roughly into two halves that mirror Washington’s geography: rugged mountains west of the Columbia River and sparse deserts to the east.

I quickly realized small-town hospitality would be my only ticket through the eastern deserts. With no infrastructure or known water on the trail for 40 miles in some areas, networking with anyone willing to provide would be key. I knew I’d be more likely to score overnight stays or solid hookups if I didn’t roll into town smelling like Sasquatch.

Early on, though, the hike took a hard turn: I limped off the trail after 60 miles with a foot injury, but decided to stay in Washington anyway. Some supportive offers from friends could give me a runway to rest up until my original bail date, and maybe hit some rock climbing if I could recover in time.

Because that plan would still require a pretty deep level of dirtbagging, I knew I could keep stink-testing my clothes—which had amazed me to this point.

The accident led to a variety of activities I wasn’t planning on.

This demanded resilience and adaptation from me and everything in my kit, including my clothes.

Apart from activities, my clothing was also subjected to heavy chemical factors, including sleeping bag sweat, dehydrated meal sweat, fried food sweat, and beer sweat. Smoky campsites, rampant use of catholes and wag bags, many cups of coffee, and trash bags packed in vans directly alongside gear during rainy spells also played a role.

In short, I believe the textile engineering of several items made it possible to keep the same clothes on my back for the duration—without disgusting myself, visibly offending service workers, or prompting any business owners to kick me out.

To understand this question is to understand why a tiny startup like HercLéon would market a copper-infused T-shirt for $130.

TL;DR: Body odor happens because our skin is a Golden Corral for bacteria. And it’s open 24 hours.

No matter what we’re doing, our skin is always generating natural oils and shedding dead cells. Glands in areas like the armpits and groin constantly leech thicker protein- and lipid-composed fluids onto the skin. The resulting buildup becomes a body-sized feeding trough for potentially trillions of bacteria.

When those bacteria expel waste, that’s where stink comes from. That and the layers of old oil, decaying cells, etc. that accumulate until you wash them off with soap and water.

Imagine flooding this system with sweat, then draping a layer of clothing on top. Sweat itself is generally odorless, but it does help bacteria multiply. And when it touches the clothing, it allows them to swim, slosh, or spill over. If your skin is a microbial Golden Corral, your sweaty clothes are like a swim-up bar attached to the dining room. But not all textiles are equally hospitable.

Polyester repels water but attracts oil. Skin oils can bond tightly to its synthetic fibers, but the fibers naturally reject water, even in the washing machine. The oil, and anything else gummed up in it, gets welded to the fabric. (This is why some of your cheapest workout shirts get “permastink.”)

Merino wool is the opposite: It repels oil and attracts water. The thirsty fibers soak up sweat from the skin, but leave most bacteria behind, stuck in the oil. And because the merino is removing their water source, the bacteria have a harder time multiplying and farting out more odor.

Techy fabrics like those from Patagonia and HercLéon take this equation of moisture and bacterial transfer to the nth degree—they seek to wall off the swim-up bar.

The HercShirt felt great right out of the bag in a size small, and matched my sizing expectations. Field performance proved to be incredible.

The fabric felt slightly heavy, sliding across my skin with a gentle pressure that felt cooling and was never scratchy. I found it fit closely enough to help me look sharp in town, but it never lost its shape. After three weeks, the material still felt stretchy everywhere. The collar hadn’t bagged out, and even the shirt’s hem under my hip belt wasn’t sagging or creased. By the end of the journey, it was tie-dyed with sweat stains from pack straps, but still passed as a deep navy blue. It never developed pit stains.

Of course, odor did become noticeable. It’s hard to say whether it was on day 12 or 20, but I also made no effort to clean the shirt. So based on my testing, HercLeon’s stated 10-day freshness target is fair—especially if you take the punishing factors of my testing field into account. My shirt endured days of sweaty hiking, exposure to muggy northwestern rainforests, late nights out on the town, cold snaps, and rainstorms that kept me layered up for days on end. It survived nights wadded up at the bottom of a sleeping bag around my heinous feet. I have almost no doubt that 10 days of normal wear with regular showers would be feasible.

My HercUnderwear 2.0 Boxer Briefs were equally impressive. With the caveat that there is a wide spectrum of underwear hygiene tolerance in the population, my findings are below.

First, did I wear the same pair of underwear every day for over three weeks without washing them? No, because there are bacterial realities that command respect. I did take a backup pair of boxer briefs, and I wrung out the HercUnderwear once in a sink with hand soap and once in the ocean. With only this spartan care, the single pair of shorts served for up to nine days at a time. (I used wet wipes consistently.)

For comparison, I did test how long I could make my spare Hanes 92/8 poly/spandex units last. I found four days was my threshold, and wanted to incinerate them after that for the benefit of the trash workers. Meanwhile, crude handwashing rejuvenated the HercUnderwear to a satisfactory extent for the field.

I found fit and roominess to be on the small side. I opted for medium with my 29-30” waist.

Ultimately, I’ll keep the underwear in my kit for activities except hot-weather hiking. The fabric is a bit heavier than many boxer briefs, and can feel slightly warming depending on pants choice.

HercLéon’s engineering exists at every level of manufacturing. Instead of using a spray-on coating, the brand mixes tiny particles of copper and charcoal into its raw textile material before spinning that into fibers. It is called a “masterbatch.” Materials are chosen to control odor at three different points: bacterial growth, odor absorption, and moisture management.

The shirt starts with lyocell, a soft, moisture-absorbing textile fiber made from processed wood pulp.

Copper particles embedded in the fibers release antimicrobial ions when damp. This damages bacterial cell walls, limiting their ability to multiply and convert sweat and other food sources into foul-smelling compounds.

The next contingency is charcoal. Their highly porous carbon structure can trap odor molecules that do develop, HercLéon says, preventing them from escaping into the air.

Finally, “plasma modification”—altering the surface properties of the fibers with ionically-charged gases during manufacturing—causes sweat to spread out and evaporate across the garment, rather than accumulate. Less lingering moisture means fewer opportunities for bacteria to multiply. HercLéon recently launched the HercSock 5 on Kickstarter, which uses the same technology that’s in the shirt and the boxer briefs. However, I did not get to test them on this trip.

Stumbling into Cle Elum, Washington, with wobbly legs, an injured foot, and a calorie deficit, I lurched toward the nearest bar (a long, long mile away). It had been a 30-mile day, and I’d been walking since it was too cold to feel my fingers in the morning. The afternoon in the sparse Yakima River valley had reached 93 degrees. I hadn’t stopped to change clothes—I knew I was hurt and no comfort would amount to real relief.

Night fell, and I sat down at a park bench in a fugue state to put on layers. I reached for my shirt collar to pull it off, expecting to wrestle with a sweat-soaked sheet. Instead, it was bone dry.

My Patagonia Capilene Cool Ultra hoody slotted into the “go-to” position on the trip. The lightest of four entries in the Capilene line, Patagonia builds it specifically for summer temperatures. I confirmed this use case in an unseasonably hot, exposed ascent of the west face of Exfoliation Dome. But I also discovered the hoody had just enough weight to take the shiver factor out of a damp Pacific morning.

Features are limited but functional. I found that using the thumb loops didn’t stretch the sleeves beyond recognition, and I liked the single button to tighten the hood. There are no pockets. Wearing the hoody roughly as much as my HercShirt, often layered with it, I got the sense that odor control wasn’t quite as strong. But it did still generally meet the limits of social acceptability by the end of the trip. And since it was easy to rinse and dried fast, I had no problem dunking it and wringing it occasionally.

According to Patagonia’s anti-stink coating provider, this shouldn’t have worked to refresh odor-fighting capabilities. The coating is a handful of botanicals arranged in a bioengineered structure. HeiQ Mint contains essential mint oils and other “naturally derived deodorizing ingredients”—inside capsules the manufacturer claims are capable of trapping the oils and acids that cause odor. This proprietary “encapsulation technology” snatches odor-causing particles and encloses them during wear. Then it releases them during washing thanks to the alkalinity of soapy water. Thus, laundering duds like the Capilene Cool hoody restores them for their next use, according to HeiQ.

On the last day of the trip, we walked down from the base of Blueberry Buttress (5.8+, 1,000 feet). In just a half mile from the foot of the climb to the car, we lost 1,300 feet of elevation. Quads screaming, we reached my borrowed van and flopped. My climbing partner wrestled himself out of his soaking wet T-shirt, now two or three sizes too big, and hung it on a tree branch.

My Capilene hoody wasn’t stinking up the campsite, and it still fit around my shoulders. Plus, it was dry enough to continue wearing comfortably.

Lunatec’s “never needs washing” camp cloths were absolutely clutch in my kit. With no technology on board except a loose weave for fast drying, the two units thoroughly supplemented wiping and cleanup needs without creating their own.

The green “odor-free” dishcloth was abrasive enough to lift stuck-on burnt bits, and highly durable. Its diffuse weave made it economical to rinse after scouring cookware with sand.

The “self-cleaning” washcloth, slightly larger and stretchier, played well for more detailed work. It was minimally absorbent (I didn’t reach for it when I spilled an entire beer into my friend’s van carpet). But viscous bits like snot or soup remnants clung to it well, then vanished when rinsed. The elastic hang tabs doubled as gathering straps, making each cloth easy to pack up.

What is Lunatec’s secret to self-cleaning? According to the brand, nothing. Their washcloths are 100% nylon, and nothing else.

A backpacker’s world is a stinky one no matter what. So if you’re on an anti-gross-out program, how can you tell if your efforts have meant anything? How can you tell if you’ve kept the Golden Corral in the corral?

There is a device used to measure odors in clinical settings called an olfactometer. It works by, basically, establishing a control smell and then upping the ante in increments—approaching the threshold where the subject can’t handle it anymore. In everyday practice, though, you experience moments when you become suddenly aware of an odor. You lift a shoulder to reach an awkward zipper or squat fast to pick up something you dropped—and the wave breaks. A solid mass of stink floods your face, and you wonder how long everyone else has been able to tell.

For many of us, that’s the trigger. “I need to wash, somehow, now.”

Over 25 days living in a pretty dirty corner of the dirtbag life, I never had that moment. River plunges sufficed for bathing. Sink water rinses refreshed the hardest workhorses in my wardrobe. I didn’t take a microscope, but I think the makers of my clothing delivered on their broad promise: Science can help you not stink (or at least, stink less).

The maintenance burden of living outside full-time had been meaningfully decreased. I thrived in my unexpected program of outdoor and social events for over three weeks with a wardrobe that would fit in a McDonald’s bag, and I’d spent zero time doomscrolling at the laundromat.

Boarding my flight, I looked down at my disheveled rags and scratched at an itch in my neck—I also hadn’t shaved for the whole trip. Then, both of my neighbors arrived and settled in, smiled warmly, and relaxed.

#8295. The Joy and Agony of the New York City Marathon’s Five-Borough 50th

The Monday before my second New York City Marathon, I was at Avenue Sky Lounge at the Peak, perched on the 101st floor of 30 Hudson Yards, for the after-party to the New York premiere of Everest: The Other Side. A good room for thinking about big climbs.

Rich Roll, the ultra-endurance athlete and podcaster, was there. We got to talking about Sunday. He admitted he was nervous. A year and a half earlier, after spinal fusion surgery, his surgeon had told him to forget about running. If a man who has built a life on going long was nervous, I figured I was allowed to be, too.

I drifted to the window to look at what we were nervous about. Far to the south, the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge, where the marathon starts, was a thin strand of light. Turn around, and there was the dark rectangle of Central Park, where it ends. In between: everything. Brooklyn, Queens, a corner of the Bronx, the long canyon of First Avenue.

You can look at the route on a map forever to try to familiarize yourself with the course and come up with a race plan—don’t bomb up or down the Verrazzano because you’ll pay for it on the Queensboro Bridge, keep it steady in Brooklyn, give it everything on Central Park South. I’d run this course before. And still, from up there, no matter how much I’d planned, I had to ask myself: I signed up for what?

Six days later, there was no backing out. At 4 A.M. on Sunday I was on the F train. This being the morning after Halloween, I had company: a car full of people in costume, Darth Vader and Rosie the Riveter among them, ending their night as I was starting my day. It was also the morning the clocks fell back. The whole city got an extra hour of sleep. Nearly 60,000 of us didn’t get to sleep in, though.

From midtown, a bus to Staten Island. Traffic on the West Side Highway, a road I’ve run hundreds of times, the site of most of my training runs. (Prospect Park’s hills would have been the smarter choice more often, if I’m honest.) Out the window, the sky over Brooklyn went purple, then pink. Brooklyn, where nearly half this race is run, has been my home for most of my life now.

They say the best thing about Jersey City is its view of Manhattan. At 6 A.M. it’s the other way around: the sun rises behind you and lands gold on Jersey City’s glass towers, which throw it back across the old Hudson.

That’s how you measure 26.2 miles in New York. By subway, by bus, on foot, from the air. And, finally, by running it.

This one was going to be special no matter what. Fifty years ago, in 1976, the marathon broke out of Central Park, where it had been run in laps, and took to the streets of all five boroughs. About 2,000 people entered that first city-wide race, only 88 of them women. This year, more than 61,000 finished, nearly 29,000 of them women.

The New York City Marathon is a place where achievement comes in many sizes, and the stories it produces are unusually varied. Andreas Almgren of Sweden won the men’s race in 2:06:01—in the first marathon of his life. Kenya’s Sheila Chepkirui won the women’s race for the second time in three years. American Jess McClain caught two-time champion Hellen Obiri in the final strides to take second, the first American on the podium here since 2018. Marcel Hug won his eighth wheelchair title; Catherine Debrunner won hers by more than eight minutes.

The stories farther back are just as good. Rich Roll made it to the start and then to the finish. Now 60, he’d trained on just two five-mile run-walks a week, careful not to push his fused spine. And he didn’t run it for himself. He served as run support for former Army Master Sergeant Cedric King, a Purple Heart recipient who lost both legs above the knee to an IED. Afterward, Roll wrote on an Instagram post that the secret to a big life is to make it about “something much larger than yourself.”

William Goodge, a British ultrarunner, crossed the line in Central Park to finish his 50th marathon in 23 days, one in every state, a run that began in Honolulu on October 9. It earned him a Guinness World Record and money for Stand Up To Cancer, in honor of his late mother.

And then there’s Dave Obelkevich, 83, who has finished every five-borough New York City Marathon since that first one in 1976. On Sunday he lined up for number 49, his daughter beside him.

This is also the rare race where watching the last finishers come in is a highlight. This year the last one home was James Thomas, 78, known to his running friends as Marty. He crossed the line around 11:20 P.M., long after the winners had probably gone to bed. It was his 43rd New York City Marathon; he ran his first in 1980.

People call marathon Sunday one of the best days in New York. The reason is community: the bands along Fourth Avenue in Bay Ridge; the hush, then the noise, through Williamsburg as if they never stopped partying from the night before; the roaring crowds when you come off the silence of Queensboro Bridge onto First Avenue; gospel in Harlem; the strangers who yell your name when you need it the most.

This year, I’d need them more than I’d hoped.

My race did not go as planned. The wheels came off on the Queensboro Bridge, as they do for so many. Even people who have never run New York know its reputation for unraveling runners’ dreams. It’s quiet. No crowds, no boost of energy. People are cursing. They’re cramping. If you feel good here, you have a fighting chance. If you don’t, you might be cooked. It turns out I was cooked. I knew I would finish, but the bridge let me know it wasn’t going to be the PR I’d hoped for.

Still, my blowup at the London Marathon in April had taught me something: If you can’t lock into the pace you want, lock into joy. So I power-walked when I had to, to keep my legs from fully cramping. But whenever a kid stuck a hand out, I ran for the high five. And when someone shouted my name with enough conviction, I started running again, as if the words were magic. The signs helped keep me entertained. The best riffed on the Elizabeth Holmes meme: “There’s only two miles to go, why would I deceive you?” (Spotted at mile 18.) And, this being New York: “Run If You Hate Wemby.”

I don’t think I have ever enjoyed Sour Patch Kids as much as the ones a pint-size candy dealer with a giant sack of them pressed into my hand at mile 21, somewhere in Harlem, with five miles still to go. Sour, then sweet.

On the subway home, draped in the orange poncho, I talked with other finishers and unpacked the day. Some were elated simply to have finished. Others were crushed by times I’d have been thrilled with. It reminded me: it isn’t about times. Mostly.

At the dinner table that night, over take-out Kung Pao chicken, my kids and I unpacked it again. I told them I wasn’t happy with my result. That I have a lot to think about in how I train for the next one. But I got it done, and I got through it mostly injury-free. (Toenail count pending.)

My younger daughter was proud of something too. At her second cross-country meet, she ran a minute and a half faster than her first. She’s learning to push herself, gently.

Then we talked about what keeps you going when things get hard. My older daughter said she reminds herself that humans were built to run. That this is what our bodies were made to do.

I’ll take that into the next training block. And be more prepared for the Queensboro Bridge.
